Each persistent failure on the left makes the operator abort the transition, and a closed gate stays closed until a dense refit restores every required receiver to the committed version. An owner that lost its state also reinitializes its baseline, drawn dashed.Some persistent failures fall outside the automatic recovery of Algorithm B.2 and require operator intervention: conflicting canonical values or destination writes, a write that bypasses the dispatch hook, a receiver that never acknowledges, or an owner that loses its candidate shards or its baseline in a crash. The operator aborts the transition: the coordinator stops and drains the attempt and cleans up, and a closed request gate stays closed until a dense refit restores every required receiver to the committed version (Figure B.6). An owner that lost its state also reinitializes its baseline, as after a source membership change.Appendix C Integration and MeasurementFigure C.1: Integration sketch. The codec, receiver checks, commit, and recovery of Algorithms B.1 and B.2 form a shared core with three interfaces: a transport adapter with three calls, conversion tasks with mapping metadata on the training side, and the serving runtime’s native loader with a dispatch hook on its final storage copies.This appendix describes the implementation behind § 3 and gives the pipeline settings for § 7.2 and measurement details for § 8. The cited NeMo RL commit [24] contains the Megatron Bridge and vLLM integration used in the experiments. Figure C.1 sketches the integration. Each transport adapter implements only , , and of Table B.1, and Appendix A.1 lists the training-side conversion tasks and mapping classes.The rollout side adds three pieces to the native loader: a call, a dispatch hook, and a staging queue. For , receivers obtain canonical names, shapes, and dtypes from the training side. The dispatch hook intercepts the loader’s final storage copies, which are operations. The receiver reserves 32 resident groups of at most eight decoded payloads, plus one separate group of at most eight payloads under assembly, for at most 264 decoded payload slots in all (Figure C.2, bottom). In asynchronous RL, a separate host staging area holds compressed payloads until . A decoder then feeds this queue in declared order while the application drains it. Figure C.2 also shows the memory that a receiver keeps beyond its resident weights.Figure C.2: Top: receiver memory beyond the resident weights Pr. The host holds the decoded staging queue and the reusable scratch that sizes for the largest canonical tensor. Dashed boxes are temporary: the compressed delta staged in asynchronous RL, and GPU buffers for active masks and optional post-apply checks. Bottom: in synchronous RL, arriving payloads are decoded into a separate group under assembly, which then joins the queue of 32 resident groups of at most eight decoded payloads, the green cells. Thus the queue plus the assembly group holds at most 264 decoded payloads. After , the receiver applies queued payloads through the native loader. A full queue makes ingestion wait and slows upstream stages. In asynchronous RL, compressed payloads wait in the dashed host staging area until . A decoder then feeds the queue while the application drains it in declared order.Owners compare source shards and convert required residual tensors in chunks, with targets of 64 MiB for object storage and 256 MiB for the relay tree, and both transports use a 512 MiB bucket target. The different chunk targets shift bucket boundaries, so the payload volumes of the two transports differ slightly in Table 4. These targets are measured in bytes of local source tensors for affine tasks and of converted canonical tensors for residual tasks, before unchanged elements are dropped. A bucket counts the full input size of each chunk that emits records. Tensors and chunks are never split, so a chunk or bucket can exceed its target. At 120B, the bucket target yields 482 payloads across 32 owners. Figure 8 illustrates both units on one owner, and Figure C.3 shows how their sizes count toward the targets.Figure C.3: Chunk and bucket sizes, with heights proportional to input bytes and dashed lines at the relay-tree chunk target of 256 MiB and the bucket target of 512 MiB. A tensor larger than both targets forms its own chunk and bucket, since tensors and chunks are never split. Arrows lead from chunks with records to the bucket that counts their full input sizes, so the unchanged chunk (∅) adds nothing to either bucket.Synthetic codec benchmark.The benchmark of § 8.2 runs PyTorch 2.14.0 on four CPU threads, with random seed 42 for the BF16 inputs and 44 for the FP32 noise. The same input and noise vectors serve all three values of a. Scaling the noise by a and adding it to the input are separate FP32 operations, and rounding precedes the bitwise comparison that selects changed words (Figure C.4). Each stream holds only little-endian 16-bit words compressed with zstd 1.5.5 at level 1. The overwrite stream decodes to the updated BF16 words, and XORing the decoded masks into the inputs gives the same words. The reduction ratios of Table 2 use exact byte counts.Figure C.4: Synthetic codec benchmark. FP32 noise and rounding turn the BF16 inputs α into β, and only the changed words enter the XOR and overwrite streams. Sizes are those of Table 2 at a=10−4.Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12BNemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55BNemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B with twice the layersTable C.1: Checkpoints of the latency runs.Table C.1 lists the BF16 checkpoints behind the 30B–1T latency points, where the 30B point is Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, not the Qwen3-30B-A3B of §§ 8.3 and 8.4. Figure C.5 shows the testbed and the transport-only full-checkpoint reference of § 8.1.Timed window and intervals.Each refit’s timed window runs from t0 to t1. At t0, the first owner begins delta construction, and at t1, the last owner finishes its baseline update after the joint commit. Refit latency is t1−t0 minus the post-apply check time. For the lower bounds of § 8.7, each compute interval runs from an operation’s start until its output is ready: change flags or locations for comparison, mapped indices and values for projection, canonical tensors for residual conversion, location and value buffers for encoding, and compressed bytes for zstd. For non-blocking operations, the interval ends when execution completes. Each relay-tree transport interval runs from payload submission until the sending endpoint, the owner’s transport endpoint, receives its queueing acknowledgment. On the relay tree, receivers stage and apply a payload only after their rollout node acknowledges its queueing, so no transport interval waits for its own payload’s staging or application. In the relay-tree latency runs, the staging queue never filled, so no interval waited for queue space either. Finalization runs from the end of the last loader application to t1. The call precedes t0, and and the gate reopening follow t1.Figure C.5: Top: latency testbed and transport-only full-checkpoint reference of § 8.1, with three of the eight nodes on each side drawn. Every training node uploads an eighth of the checkpoint to S3 concurrently, and every rollout node then downloads all of it in parallel across the dashed cluster boundary. Each node’s cross-cluster flow is up to 5 Gbps. Bottom: timed window of one refit. Thin boxes are intervals, and thick strips are their unions, which count overlaps once and exclude gaps. The longest union over owners gives the construction lower bound, and the longest union over sending endpoints gives the transport lower bound.Each lower bound is the longest union of intervals on one owner or sending endpoint: the construction lower bound takes the union of each owner’s compute intervals, and the transport lower bound takes the union of each sending endpoint’s transport intervals. Before taking unions, we map Nsight Systems trace timestamps onto a common time axis and clip each interval to [t0,t1], discarding empty intersections. Each union lies within the refit’s timed window, so both bounds are at most t1−t0. We compute bounds per refit and average them as § 8.1 averages refit latency. Mean refit latency, which already excludes the post-apply check time, exceeds both mean bounds at every traced size. Figure C.5 illustrates both bounds in synchronous RL, and its receivers row shows the loader applications before finalization.For §§ 4, 5, and 7.1, this appendix details coverage, the payload format, and payload volume.The XOR/overwrite split follows the mapping classes of Appendix A.1 and the loader paths of Appendix A.2. On the default BF16 paths, each owned shard of an affine tensor contributes one XOR item when it has changed elements and its path is representation-preserving with no overlapping writes. Each required residual tensor emits an overwrite item when its converted bits change. Figure D.1 summarizes the rule and shows why scaled and cast values need overwrites.Figure D.1: Top: encoding of a record in the default mixed mode. All conditions are decided in advance for each mapping class and loader path. Bottom: a source XOR mask under a conversion that scales by 1.5 and casts to BF16. The example element’s mask is, but the mask of its converted values and is , so the source mask cannot update the converted bits, which need an overwrite.Mamba input projection and convolutionEmbedding and output headTable D.1: Affine and residual canonical tensors in Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B. The Bytes column gives shares of the 1,121 GB checkpoint, with one share for the three residual rows together. Other affine weights include shared experts, routers, latent-MoE projections, attention output projections, normalization, and the output projections and state parameters of Mamba.Direct-projection coverage.Table D.1 shows that affine mappings cover all but 185 canonical tensors of the Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B checkpoint, which has no custom export hook. Routed experts use qualifying per-expert Auto mappings. Of the 185 residual tensors, 183 have mappings outside the supported classes: the Mamba input projections and convolutions, and attention Q/K/V, including those of the multi-token-prediction layer. The remaining two residual tensors are the embedding and output head. For Qwen3-30B-A3B, Table D.2 counts 18,721 of the 18,867 canonical tensors as affine. Its residual tensors are attention Q/K/V and the embedding and output head.Attention output projectionEmbedding and output headTable D.2: Affine and residual canonical tensors in Qwen3-30B-A3B. The Bytes column gives each weight type’s share of the 61.06 GB checkpoint.For the Qwen3-30B-A3B checkpoint of Table D.2, when every tensor and shard changes, XOR covers 18,721 of 18,867 items at tensor-parallel and expert-tensor-parallel degree one, 74,161 of 74,307 at degree four, and 148,081 of 148,227 at degree eight. Each of the 18,432 expert tensors and 48 attention output projections splits into t shards at degree t, while the 48 router and 193 normalization tensors stay whole, giving 18,480​t+241 XOR items (Figure D.2). The XOR share of weight bytes stays 96.3% because a higher degree only splits the same weights into more shards.Figure D.2: XOR items of Qwen3-30B-A3B at tensor-parallel and expert-tensor-parallel degree t, drawn for t=4. Each expert tensor and attention output projection splits into t shards, one item each, while each router and normalization tensor stays whole as one item.For the Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B checkpoint of Table D.1, when every tensor and shard changes, 403,869 of the 404,054 items are affine at tensor-parallel and expert-tensor-parallel degree eight. Each of the 50,176 routed expert up/down tensors splits into te shards at expert-tensor-parallel degree te, and 257 of the 662 other affine tensors split into t shards at tensor-parallel degree t, while the remaining 405 stay whole, giving 50,176​te+257​t+405 affine items and 185 residual items. Every affine item takes the XOR path except those of the few Mamba state parameters that the native loader transforms, so the XOR share of weight bytes still rounds to the 97.0% affine share.Each payload carries attempt, owner, and payload identifiers, flat location and value buffers, and per-item metadata: tensor name, shape, dtype, encoding, location type, and offsets into both buffers. Contiguous locations use a start index, and the number of values gives the run length. Scattered locations use gaps in the smallest suitable integer type. A BLAKE2b-128 digest [1] covers each compressed payload body.Figure D.3 illustrates the payload format with two tensors. The changed elements of tensor A form one contiguous run, so its metadata row stores a start index instead of location offsets and adds nothing to the location buffer. Tensor B’s scattered positions are stored as gaps. Both rows index the shared value buffer.Figure D.3: Top: payload format. To decode gaps, start at −1 and add each gap plus one: gaps 2, 2, 2 yield positions 2, 5, 8. Values have the width of their tensor’s dtype. Bottom: quantities behind payload volume. Owners find Nchg changes among Nsrc source elements, which gives the element change rate ssrc. The emitted destinations D contain the changed destinations Dchg, whose share of the N canonical elements is the canonical change density s. When a mapping is not a representation-preserving bijection, D can also hold an unchanged destination, drawn outlined. Payloads carry metadata, locations, and values, and with Nnode rollout nodes, object storage moves about (1+Nnode)​Vpayload per attempt in uploads and downloads.To relate payload bytes to the element change rate (Figure D.3), let Ω be the full canonical index set and N=|Ω|. Because ownership is disjoint, N_{\mathrm{src}}=\sum_{T}|J_{T}| counts unique source elements and N_{\mathrm{chg}}=\sum_{T}|C_{T}| counts unique changes. The element change rate is ssrc=Nchg/Nsrc. The emitted destinations form D=\bigcup_{T\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{aff}}}\pi_{T}(C_{T})\cup\bigcup_{u\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{req}}}D_{u}. The destinations with changed canonical bits form Dchg={d∈Ω∣I​(Wv+1)d≠I​(Wv)d}, and complete change detection makes it a subset of D. The canonical change density is s=|Dchg|/N. The element change rate and the canonical change density are equal when a representation-preserving bijection maps source elements to canonical elements.Before zstd, the payloads of one attempt together carry metadata, run- and gap-coded locations, and one value per record. Let be the canonical checkpoint size, where bd is the width of element d in bytes. With one record per emitted destination, the value bytes total , which at uniform width is |D|​H/N, or s​H when D=Dchg. Here D counts unique destinations. Each additional overwrite record for a destination adds another bd bytes. More scattered changes need more location bytes, and more items need more metadata. After zstd compresses the locations and values, the attempt’s payloads total Vpayload. On the object-storage transport, each attempt moves about (1+Nnode)​Vpayload of upload and download traffic when Nnode rollout nodes download every payload. On the relay tree without retransmission, each payload crosses the cluster boundary once per attempt, so cross-cluster traffic is about Vpayload, and the root forwards each payload over local links to every rollout node.Appendix E GRPO Experiment SettingsThis appendix details the GRPO settings for the element-change measurements in § 2.2 and for the training runs in § 8.4.Figure E.1: Receiver kills in one NeMo-DCR run of § 8.4, with an illustrative choice of instances. Every five steps, a randomly chosen vLLM instance is killed mid-refit at a cross and restarted five steps later, at a dot, where it restores the committed version.Element-change measurements.These measurements follow the agentic SWE RL recipe for Qwen3 [25]: BF16 weights, FP32 AdamW state, constant learning rate 10−6, and no warmup, weight decay, or KL penalty. The six measured models are Qwen3-30B-A3B, Llama-3.2-3B, Gemma-3-4B, and Qwen2.5 at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 7B.These runs use the first stage of the same recipe, with from the Nemotron-RL-Super-Training-Blends dataset. This stage rewards single-step tool calls for matching the arguments of the expert action. Each GRPO step uses 64 prompts with 8 responses each and a batch size of 512. With and , probability ratios are clipped to [0.8,1.28]. The logged estimates the per-token KL divergence between rollout and training policies. Figure E.1 shows the receiver kills.This appendix gives the evidence behind each mark of Table 1 under requirements G1–G5 of § 2.3, and the same analysis for the slime framework.The design meets all five requirements. § 6.2 and Appendix A establish G1, and the dense-refit comparisons of § 8.1 confirm it. For G2, the payload volumes of Tables 3 and 4 scale with the changed set. For G3, placement stays in the native loader with no model-specific logic, as §§ 6.1 and 8.1 describe. For G4, both transports deliver without a cross-cluster collective, as § 7 describes, and the latency runs of § 8.1 use them between clusters that share no InfiniBand or EFA route. Payload deduplication, overwrite recovery, and joint commit meet G5, as § 6.3 and Appendix B describe, and with receivers killed mid-refit, both transports follow dense NCCL’s mean reward and KL trajectories in Figure 9.Approaches A and B fully meet G1, and approach D avoids arithmetic reconstruction but meets G1 only partly. NCCL-Reshard and checkpoint-engine send every weight rather than a delta, so they preserve the target bits [22, 20]. TensorHub copies its published buffers into the serving runtime’s registered tensors, which yields exact target bits because the published buffers hold the weights in the layout and dtype of the registered tensors [40]. PULSE’s Appendix H.6 proves exact reconstruction of a tensor from a correct base [19], but extending the proof through a native loader requires conditions on the loader’s transformations and storage writes. In verl, NaN masks in intercepted copies protect unchanged positions, and a round-trip test checks that the model’s generated outputs are bit-identical [36], but the loader’s supported transformations are not stated. SparseRL-Sync patches the loader’s copy with a NaN-masked sparse scatter and reports tensor-by-tensor bitwise agreement with a dense refit, but does not specify supported transformations or interception of every storage write [11]. NeMo-DCR specifies both in the loader conditions of § 6.1 and Appendix A.2, and Appendix A proves that under these conditions its refits produce the same bits as a dense refit.In approach C, arithmetic reconstruction of updated or pre-update values can introduce rounding errors. ROSE sends arithmetic differences [6]. AuroraRL reports lossless reconstruction by scatter-adding deltas but does not state when this reconstruction is bit-exact [30]. AReaL-DTE [26] reconstructs pre-update weights by inverting AdamW and compares BF16 bit patterns after aligning them to a common layout. Its authors note rounding in fused AdamW implementations, so comparison against these reconstructed pre-update weights can miss a changed element. NeMo-DCR instead compares against stored values retained in the committed source baseline.Approaches A and B move every weight byte, while the delta schemes in approaches C and D scale with the changed set. PULSE, SparseRL-Sync, and verl in approach D send absolute overwrites as indices and values of changed elements, with BF16 values in PULSE and verl. The verl framework detects changes on each training rank’s shard and maps them to full-tensor coordinates through block placements, and it supports conversions only when they permute elements [35, 36]. AReaL-DTE sends target values of detected changes, and AuroraRL packages each step as a BF16 delta checkpoint.The serving runtime performs all weight placement in checkpoint-engine, SparseRL-Sync, and verl, and only part of it in NCCL-Reshard and TensorHub. In checkpoint-engine, the serving runtime also chooses which weights to copy. NCCL-Reshard copies expert feed-forward shards directly into vLLM parameters using its own placement metadata and hooks. Only the remaining parameters pass through the native loader, so native placement is partial. TensorHub copies its published buffers into the serving runtime’s registered tensors without interpreting their layout. Yet weights are converted to the rollout layout before publication, not by the native loader, so native placement is only partial [40].Most delta systems place updates themselves. ROSE uses shard-aware routing to receiver shards, and AuroraRL writes directly into parameter storage. PULSE writes values at the transmitted indices into receiver tensors that share the sender’s layout. AReaL-DTE remaps updates into rollout layouts at the receiver and uses the native loader only as a fallback, so its native placement is partial.NCCL-Reshard, SparseRL-Sync, and verl each use a collective that spans training and rollout. The checkpoint-engine system runs alongside serving runtimes, loads full weights onto GPUs from disk or the training engine, and broadcasts them among its workers. Its description mentions no cross-cluster transport [20]. PULSE, AReaL-DTE, ROSE, AuroraRL, and TensorHub transfer weights through replication, relays, or shared storage without a cross-cluster collective. TensorHub pipelines its full-weight replication, placing one replica in each remote datacenter before replicating locally. AuroraRL streams each delta checkpoint through one seed actor per region.No existing system in Table 1 fully meets G5. ROSE, SparseRL-Sync, and verl describe no recovery protocol, although verl does checksum each broadcast payload. For NCCL-Reshard and checkpoint-engine, repeating a dense refit can restore weights, but the cited descriptions do not specify a complete protocol for partial failures and policy commit. TensorHub provides transactions, invalidates incomplete replicas, and recovers transfers from another source [40], but it coordinates version selection within each model-parallel group rather than committing across all required receivers. AReaL-DTE commits a version manifest and leaves partially applied versions to its control plane, without describing their repair. AuroraRL checks the version a delta applies to, uses leases for fault handling, stages deltas before activation, and lets lagging actors replay the delta chain, but does not describe repair after partial writes.PULSE receivers advance independently, without committing the source baseline and the required receivers’ policy version together. PULSE’s Algorithm 5 checks the local version before decoding [19], and a receiver applies consecutive deltas directly. PULSE also keeps periodic full checkpoints called anchors. After missed versions, the receiver restores a ready anchor and replays subsequent deltas in order. Ready markers prevent use of incomplete uploads, and a full-state hash checks each reconstruction before the new weights are returned. A mismatch triggers anchor recovery. Absolute overwrites can be repeated safely, and anchor restoration replaces a partially applied state.The slime framework’s delta weight sync publishes byte-level XOR or overwrite deltas of the gathered Hugging Face tensors to a shared filesystem [33]. Each rollout node patches a full local checkpoint, verifies per-tensor checksums, and reloads the checkpoint from disk through the native loader. This design meets G1–G4, but every refit reads the full model. It does not fully meet G5: the trainer advances its source baseline before any rollout node applies the published version, and no commit ties the baseline to the version that the rollout nodes hold.HackerNoon is republishing this paper in full for the record, with credit to all of its authors. It was originally published on arXiv as arXiv:2610.08430 under a CC BY 4.0 license. The original title appears above. HackerNoon added a new headline and adapted the formatting from arXiv's HTML version. The paper's text, figures, tables and references are otherwise unchanged.

item.title: HyprBSD Provides Wayland-Based Desktop Built Atop FreeBSD, Complete With Steam Gaming
item.author: Michael Larabel
item.content:encoded: While FreeBSD has been working to improve its desktop and laptop experience, that work isn't yet shipping in released form for the OS installer and other ongoing efforts. Now there's a new desktop FreeBSD distribution on the scene with HyprBSD providing a Wayland-based desktop experience and with the Linux binary compatibility layer even an easy route to gaming with Steam...

item.title: Software You Never Set Up Is Money You Wasted: How Firstep Configures the Dashboard for You
item.author: Sanya Kapoor
item.content:encoded: There is a particular kind of waste that almost every small business has paid for. An owner signs up for a promising piece of software, logs in, and finds a blank screen waiting to be configured. Fields to define, settings to choose, workflows to build. The owner, who has actual work to do, closes the tab and tells themselves they will set it up this weekend. They never do. The subscription renews anyway, month after month, for a tool that was never once used.This is the hidden failure of most business software. The problem is rarely the features. It is the setup, the hours of configuration that stand between buying a tool and getting anything out of it, and that solo owners almost never have the time or patience to finish.Why the Blank Dashboard WinsA customer relationship manager is the clearest example. Owners are told, correctly, that a CRM keeps a business organized by tracking customers and sales, sending reminders, handling quotes and invoices, and keeping every conversation in one place. All of that is true, and none of it matters if the system sits empty because no one built it out. An unconfigured CRM is just a more expensive spreadsheet that the owner is afraid to open.The reason the blank dashboard usually wins is simple math. Setup is front-loaded work with a delayed payoff. The owner has to invest hours now, learning the software and entering the structure of their business, in exchange for benefits that only show up later. Faced with that trade-off against a day already full of paying work, most owners defer, and deferral quietly becomes never.Setting It Up for the Owner Instead, a Dayton, Ohio company, takes the opposite approach by doing the configuration before the owner ever logs in. Its CRM arrives already built, with the company describing the result plainly: the business starts organized, professional, and easy to manage from day one. Rather than handing over an empty system, Firstep sets it up so the owner inherits a working dashboard instead of a project.The part that makes this practical is the industry-specific automations. A generic CRM has to be told what a business does. Firstep’s comes pre-configured for the owner’s trade, with templates, workflows, and funnels relevant to that specific line of work already in place. A cleaning business and a catering business do not get the same blank canvas; they get dashboards shaped around how each actually operates. A landscaper might log in to find lead pipelines, booking workflows, and follow-up sequences already built for recurring seasonal service, rather than a set of empty fields asking what a pipeline should contain. That pre-configuration is the difference between a tool the owner has to translate into their business and one that already speaks their language.“Small business owners shouldn’t have to become software experts just to run their business,” a Firstep spokesperson said. “We want to eliminate that learning curve by helping set up the tools and automations they need from the start. Instead of spending hours figuring out how to make everything work, they can focus on what matters most — growing their business.”Why This Is the Feature That Decides the RestSetup sounds like a minor convenience. For a solo owner, it is actually the gatekeeper for everything else. A dashboard that is never configured is a dashboard whose payment tools, scheduling, follow-ups, and reminders all go unused too, because the owner never got far enough in to reach them. Solve the setup, and the rest of the platform becomes reachable. Leave it unsolved, and the most capable software in the world is just another renewing charge for a login no one visits.Firstep bundles this done-for-you configuration into the same $97-per-month plan that handles formation and compliance, which reframes what the monthly fee buys. The money buys more than a set of tools. It buys tools someone has already made usable. The company says more than half of its orders since early 2024 have included ongoing services, which suggests owners stay when the software actually works in their day rather than waiting on a weekend of setup that never arrives.The waste was never that small business owners bought bad software. It was that they bought good software and never crossed the gap between signing up and using it. Firstep’s wager is that the gap is the real product, and that an owner who logs in to a dashboard already built for their trade will use it, while an owner who logs in to a blank one will quietly pay for it and walk away.

item.title: Wallet Evolution: Why Institutional Digital Assets Need More Than Secure Keys?
item.author: Sanya Kapoor
item.content:encoded: Digital-asset wallets have evolved alongside the industry they serve. Initially designed to store assets and authorize transactions, they have developed into enterprise infrastructure supporting increasingly complex financial operations. As banks and other institutions enter the market, however, the requirements extend beyond secure key management. Institutions must also demonstrate control over access, authorization, asset movements, and operational records.This shift is shaping’s expansion from MPC-based self-custody wallets into institutional asset management and custody. Founded in 2017, the digital-asset infrastructure company has developed Trust Vault, a governance framework for institutional operations, and expanded into custody.We spoke with Aaron Zhang, co-founder of Cregis and CTO of Cregis Custody FZE, who has worked on digital-asset products since 2015, about the evolution of wallet infrastructure, the changing requirements of institutional custody, and the technology needed to support them.Q: You began working on digital-asset products in 2015. What drew you to the industry, and how has your approach to building technology evolved?My interest in economic systems began long before I entered the technology industry. I was curious about fundamental questions such as why money exists and how economic exchange works. With a background in science, I pursued computer science rather than economics, but that interest in underlying systems remained.In 2015, my team began developing digital-asset products, initially focusing on wallets and Web3 tools. Over the years, the industry has changed considerably, and so have the problems we work on.I have always viewed technology as a means of solving practical problems rather than an end in itself. Building a technically sophisticated product is not enough; it must address a genuine operational need. This has become particularly relevant as digital assets move from individual ownership into institutional financial operations.Q: How have wallet requirements changed as the digital-asset industry has matured?The most significant change is in the nature of the assets being managed and the responsibilities involved.Early wallets primarily served individuals, for whom protecting private keys and preventing asset theft were the central concerns. As businesses adopted digital assets, wallets had to support multiple users, differentiated permissions, and more structured transaction management. became an important foundation for this transition by distributing key control and reducing reliance on a single point of compromise.Institutional adoption has introduced another layer of complexity. Exchanges, fintech companies, and banks increasingly manage assets on behalf of clients and other stakeholders, rather than simply holding their own funds. Their requirements therefore extend beyond asset protection to include internal controls, authorization procedures, and accountability.A wallet is no longer simply a place to store assets or sign transactions. It increasingly functions as part of an organization's broader asset-management infrastructure.Q: Why is private-key security alone insufficient for institutional asset management?Institutions must demonstrate not only that assets are secure but also that their management follows established rules.For a company handling client assets, important questions include who can initiate transactions, who must approve them, who can modify whitelists and authorization policies, and whether any individual can bypass internal controls. If an irregular transaction occurs, the institution must also be able to establish what happened and trace the decision-making process.This is particularly important for organizations subject to external audits and regulatory oversight. A secure key-management mechanism cannot, by itself, establish whether transactions comply with internal policies or whether access privileges have been appropriately controlled.The integrity of the governance framework matters just as much as the security of the assets. Even a well-designed approval process is ineffective if privileged users can modify its rules without authorization. Institutional security must therefore encompass access management, transaction authorization, policy protection, and auditability.Q: How does Cregis Trust Vault address these requirements? began researching institutional access-management mechanisms in 2022 and developed the in 2024. Its purpose is to translate an organization's internal policies into enforceable controls over digital-asset operations.Institutions can define role-based permissions, establish approval requirements for transactions, and determine who is authorized to modify those policies. Controls can also vary according to transaction amounts and risk levels, allowing organizations to apply stricter oversight to higher-risk operations without unnecessarily complicating routine transfers.One important design principle is . Before approving a transaction, an operator must be able to review its exact contents, which must correspond to the transaction ultimately executed. This helps prevent discrepancies between what an operator authorizes and what the system processes.Trust Vault also protects the integrity of the governance rules themselves. Without safeguards against unauthorized changes, access controls and approval workflows could be circumvented from within the organization.The distinction is fundamental: Cregis Trust Vault is not simply a key-storage solution. It provides a governance framework for determining who can access and move assets, under what conditions, and how those operations can be verified and audited.Q: Why is Cregis expanding from self-custody wallets into institutional custody?The expansion reflects the changing requirements of the market. As banks and other regulated businesses enter the digital-asset sector, not all have the technical capabilities or operational experience to manage assets independently.Self-custody infrastructure can meet many enterprise requirements, but institutions operating under regulatory oversight may need additional assurance around asset management, operational controls, and independent verification. Depending on their business model and regulatory obligations, they may require a formal custody arrangement involving an independent provider.For Cregis, custody builds on capabilities developed through years of working with digital-asset businesses. Trust Vault provides the governance foundation, while our experience in wallet infrastructure and institutional operations informs the broader custody offering.I see this as an extension of the same underlying objective: ensuring that digital assets are not only protected but also managed within a framework of clearly defined responsibilities and verifiable controls.As institutional participation grows, wallet infrastructure will increasingly be judged not only by how securely it manages private keys but also by how effectively it supports the governance, accountability, and operational requirements of financial institutions. is a digital asset infrastructure platform, providing technology for digital asset collections, payouts, and fund operations. Its offerings include wallet infrastructure, fund flow orchestration, and regulated custody capabilities. These solutions help businesses manage digital assets with greater security, efficiency, and control. Founded in 2017, Cregis serves financial institutions, payment service providers (PSPs), foreign exchange (Forex) brokers, fintechs, and Web3 businesses. The company operates across Asia, the Middle East, and Latin America. Today, Cregis supports more than 4,000 businesses across over 50 countries.

item.title: Cryosphere Faces Permanent Damage When World Overshoots 1.5C, Scientists Warn
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
A UN-backed report warns that even temporarily overshooting the Paris agreement's 1.5C warming target could cause permanent and widespread losses of glaciers, snow and polar ice sheets. With Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets already melting about six times faster than in the 1990s, the report argues that global temperatures should ultimately be brought back below 1C. The Guardian reports: The report, which comes as world leaders and diplomats converge on Turkey for the 31st annual Cop climate conference, documented rapid and accelerating melting of the cryosphere and polar oceans, with damages that range from the loss of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, driving sea level rises that threaten hundreds of millions of people, to thawing permafrost, which releases more planet-heating gas. Glaciers, which are still responding to historical warming, would only preserve about 70% of their current volume over a timescale of centuries if long-term heating were brought back down to 0.8C, the report found.
Meanwhile, the ice sheets covering Greenland and Antarctica, which are melting about six times faster today than in the 1990s, would continue to lose ice even in scenarios where overshoot is brief and temperature rise returns to 1.5C, the report found. The scientists said a safe, long-term temperature limit for polar ice sheets lies much closer to 1.0C of global heating, and possibly even lower. "Snow and ice respond rapidly to every fraction of a degree of warming," said [James Kirkham, a glaciologist at ICCI and the lead author of the report. "But most of these systems will take centuries or millennia to recover after overshoot, especially if tipping points are crossed that cause changes to become essentially irreversible."
Last month, a UNEP report found the world must cut emissions by 18% by 2030 and by 45% by 2035 to have a good chance of keeping temperatures from rising 1.7C above preindustrial levels. It found there were "no good outcomes" of remaining above 1.5C. The cryosphere report found that current policies, which will result in 2.8C of global heating, would reduce the mass of glacier ice to below 10% in the Rockies, Alps, Iceland and Scandinavia. If warming was limited to 1.5C, about 20-35% of the mass would remain. In the Hindu Kush Himalayas, where glaciers are a source of water for nearly a quarter of humanity, current policies will leave just 41% of the ice mass. If warming was limited to 1.5C, 83% would remain.

item.title: Insignary Releases Free Insignary-Chk Tool to Detect PHP2Shell and Node2Shell Exposure
item.author: CyberNewswire
item.content:encoded: Toronto, Canada, November 6th, 2026/CyberNewswire/--Free, read-only scanner helps organizations find Linux servers and container images exposed to two actively exploited vulnerabilities in PHP and Node.js, a global open-source security company, today released insignary-chk, a free tool that checks for PHP2Shell and Node2Shell, two recently disclosed runtime vulnerabilities affecting PHP and Node.js.PHP2Shell refers to two vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), each rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code remotely. Servers that handle web requests with PHP are at risk, including deployments using Apache mod_php, PHP-FPM, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The PHP Project released fixes on October 21, 2026, in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and earlier have reached end of life and no longer receive official releases. Because the flaws sit in the runtime itself rather than in application code, code review alone cannot reveal them, so organizations also need to find PHP instances bundled inside vendor software and container images.Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) is an out-of-bounds write flaw in Google’s Brotli decompression library, which Node.js bundles. Specially crafted compressed data can crash an affected application, expose its memory, or allow remote code execution. The issue is fixed in Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Node.js’s official end-of-life policy treats any unsupported branch (e.g., 20.x and earlier) as carrying ongoing risk once support ends, since no further security fixes are issued. insignary-chk reflects this by design: it does not flag EOL branches like Node.js 20.x as “Likely vulnerable”; instead, it surfaces them as “Check with OS vendor” when installed from a Linux distribution package, or “Unable to determine” when installed from nodejs.org or built from source, so administrators can verify the actual patch status with their vendor or upgrade to a supported release. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added both PHP2Shell and Node2Shell to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.insignary-chk is a single file that requires no installation or registration. It is read-only by default: it only reads files, never runs what it finds, and makes no changes unless the user chooses the --fix option. It sends no data over the network, except when the user chooses an option that connects to an address they specify.Because Node2Shell originates in the Brotli library, insignary-chk also checks Brotli copies outside Node.js, including the system Brotli library and Python’s brotli package. End-of-life PHP versions are likewise flagged for review against the Linux distribution’s security advisory, or for upgrade to a supported release. Results are ranked by priority, so teams can see at a glance which issues need urgent attention.The report’s to-do list is sorted by urgency: “Act now” for vulnerable files in use by a running process, “Fix soon” for vulnerable software that is installed but not running, and “Review” for items that need a manual check, followed by detailed findings for each server or container image.insignary-chk complements the Insignary Clarity product family. Insignary Clarity uses the company’s patented binary software composition analysis (SCA) to identify components and versions inside compiled applications, firmware, IT infrastructure, and container images, without requiring source code. Insignary Clarity SC brings results from Clarity, Clarity AIR, third-party SCA tools, and imported SBOMs (software bills of materials) into one platform, and maps newly disclosed CVEs to existing SBOMs without rescanning. Users who already run Clarity can use insignary-chk’s --clarity option to confirm its findings with binary analysis on their own Clarity server.“PHP2Shell and Node2Shell sit in the runtime, not in application code, so reviewing source code alone won’t show whether you’re exposed,” said Taek Wan Kim, President & CEO of Insignary. “We built insignary-chk so any organization can check its Linux servers and containers within minutes, without making changes to its systems, and focus first on the issues that matter most.”insignary-chk is available as a free download, with no sign-up required, at www.insignary.com/free-tools/php2shell-node2shell-checker. It runs on Linux x86_64 and checks only the three CVEs listed above. Windows, macOS, and arm64 are not yet supported.Insignary Inc. is a Toronto-based cybersecurity company specializing in binary composition analysis and software supply chain security. Its patented technology enables organizations to identify open-source software components, vulnerabilities, and software provenance directly from compiled binaries without requiring access to source code. The company serves enterprises, governments, and software vendors worldwide and is backed by strategic investors and partners including BearingPoint in Europe, Cybertrust Japan and TechMatrix in Japan, and TMA Solutions. Through its global partner ecosystem, Insignary supports software supply chain security initiatives across North America, Europe, and Asia. For more information, visit .ContactPrincipal Solutions ArchitectThis story was published as a press release by Cybernewswire 6under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging

item.title: Vibrating Mattress Helps Clear Alzheimer's Protein From the Brain
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
A vibrating mattress combined with two pills that release nitric oxide enhanced the brain's ability to clear an Alzheimer's-related protein. According to New Scientist, the experiment "caused the brain's blood vessels to swell and constrict more strongly, which enhanced the glymphatic system's clearance of [the protein]." From the report: [Kesa Kiviniemi at the University of Oulu in Finland] and his colleagues recruited 29 adults who hadn't been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease or any other cognitive issues. The participants took a pill that dissolves when under the tongue, releasing nitric oxide. They then lay on a mattress that caused their bodies to gently vibrate for 40 minutes, taking another pill halfway through. Blood samples revealed that their levels of a type of protein called beta-amyloid 42 increased by 35 per cent, on average, after the intervention. This protein, which usually helps neurons signal and connect to each other, misfolds and form clumps in Alzheimer's disease.
"The treatment seemed to enhance the glymphatic system's ability to clear beta-amyloid from the brain to the blood," says Kiviniemi. "A 35 per cent increase in circulating beta-amyloid 42 is a substantial and very interesting acute effect," says Tuomas Lilius at the University of Helsinki, who wasn't involved in the work. "It is certainly possible it could become biologically, and eventually clinically, relevant." Side effects were mild and minimal, with six of the participants experiencing issues such as nausea and headache. However, this could partly be due to the expectation of an effect from the nitric oxide pills. The researchers hope to overcome this in future work by including placebo pills.
Brain scans suggest the treatment enhanced the flow of fluid along glymphatic channels, probably by widening the brain's blood vessels and making them pump more strongly, says Kiviniemi. But other mechanisms could also be at play, says Brown. For instance, this intervention may slow the breakdown of beta-amyloid 42 by the liver, leading to higher amounts in the bloodstream, he says. Future studies could get around this by injecting markers into cerebrospinal fluid, which moves through the glymphatic system, to more directly measure its flow, says Brown. Additional experiments by Kiviniemi and his colleagues tested either only the mattress vibrations or only the nitric oxide pills on the same participants, at least a week before or after they underwent the combined approach. Based on brain scans, these solo interventions seemed to have less than half the effect on the glymphatic system than when they were combined. The findings have been published in the journal Nature Communications.

item.title: Before Moving Contracts Into Revenue Hub, Prove Who Will Send the Next Invoice.
item.author: Pratik Thakker
item.content:encoded: Hero image: Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.Importing a contract and moving its billing are different operations. A team can reproduce an agreement's dates and line items accurately while leaving two systems prepared to charge for the same future period.That is why a Revenue Hub migration should begin with the next invoice, not with the import file. The most consequential question is which system owns each future billing instruction, especially when the customer renews, expands, or changes terms during the transition.Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.I would treat contract migration as a controlled transfer of responsibility. A successful import is one piece of evidence. The full acceptance test is whether the team can explain the active agreement, the next bill, the collection method, and the system responsible for each action without creating duplicates or losing history.Separate visibility from billing ownershipHubSpot's direct-contract guide documents direct creation and import under a beta path. It distinguishes ordinary imports without billing schedules from a separate billing-continuity migration path. It also documents billing and collection configuration. Do not treat a record import as proof that recurring billing has moved.The implementation model below is a proposal. Example registers, states, and test cases are not native HubSpot objects or a claim that every account can perform the same migration. Verify supported paths, eligibility, payment processing, and permissions in the account before planning a production cutover.A visibility-only contract can be valuable. It can give customer-facing teams a view of the agreement while the established billing system remains authoritative. That is a legitimate architecture if the boundary is explicit and the record does not misleadingly suggest that HubSpot owns collection.Build a responsibility registerFor every agreement in scope, record the authoritative system for commercial terms, billing schedule, invoice issuance, collection, adjustments, and accounting export. Include a named owner and the evidence required to transfer each responsibility.Do not use a single migration-complete flag for all six. A contract may be visible in HubSpot while collection remains external. An accounting connector may be reconciled while payment-method transfer is still unresolved. Those are separate states, not minor details beneath one green status.An illustrative register might contain:Terms and associations checkedMethod and authorization verifiedCorrection trail retainedThe chosen owner may remain the same for some rows. Migration does not have to mean moving every responsibility at once. It does require avoiding two active owners for one billable obligation.Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.Capture the agreement as of a defined checkpoint. Include customer identity, billing entity, currency, term dates, recurring and one-time items, billing cadence, open invoices, approved adjustments, renewal terms, and pending amendments.The baseline should distinguish committed terms from disputed or proposed changes. A salesperson's planned expansion is not an accepted amendment. A draft renewal is not the next active contract. An overdue invoice is not a reason to rewrite the commercial record to match the collected amount.Reconcile the baseline with the people authorized to interpret it. Technical teams should not invent the treatment of unusual terms or decide how revenue should be recognized. Route accounting and legal questions to the appropriate owners, while documenting the resulting implementation decisions.Freeze only the scope necessary for the cutover, and specify how urgent changes will be handled. An undocumented freeze creates shadow updates. A controlled exception process can preserve continuity without pretending the business will stop changing for the convenience of an import.Classify amendments as dated revisionsAn expansion, contraction, date correction, billing-contact update, and renewal are not interchangeable edits. Classify the change before choosing the mechanism that applies it.HubSpot's contract overview describes change quotes and direct-edit paths with different requirements. It also states that an accepted renewal quote creates a new contract associated with the prior one. Those lifecycle relationships should be preserved rather than flattened into a single continually overwritten record.For a hypothetical expansion, retain the agreement before the change, the approved amendment, the effective date, the affected line items, and the expected billing consequence. A proposed amendment can have a future effective date without changing what the customer owes for the current period.Use separate evidence for agreement acceptance and system execution. The customer may approve a change before the billing system applies it. Conversely, a system edit may occur without sufficient business approval. Both mismatches should be visible in an exception queue.Prove proration with fixtures, not intuitionProration is a policy implemented through software. The result can depend on effective dates, billing periods, currencies, rounding, credits, and the treatment of previously issued invoices. A short arithmetic formula is not enough to describe every commercial arrangement.HubSpot's contract setup documentation includes proration and renewal settings. Verify the actual configuration and supported behavior before modeling expected results. Do not assume an example from another account proves your account's outcome.Build synthetic fixtures for a mid-period increase, a mid-period decrease, a future-dated change, a change near a renewal boundary, and a change after an invoice has already been issued. For each fixture, finance should approve the expected commercial treatment before the engineering test is judged.Retain the calculation inputs and expected document sequence. When a result differs, classify whether the issue is a setting, an unsupported scenario, an incorrect expectation, or an implementation defect. Do not repair a test by manually changing the total until it looks plausible.Keep invoice corrections and contract changes distinctA billing correction does not necessarily amend the agreement. A contract amendment does not necessarily explain every historical invoice correction. Keeping both records prevents the team from erasing the distinction.The contract management guide allows editing eligible manually associated invoices, but excludes subscription-created invoices and invoices automatically associated after quote acceptance. An eligible invoice amount edit does not update total contract value. That separation should inform reconciliation rather than be treated as a defect to eliminate through forced synchronization.For example, imagine a hypothetical billing error that is corrected without changing the customer's agreed package. The correction trail should explain the invoice adjustment while leaving the approved commitment intact. If the customer also negotiated a package reduction, that is a second business event with its own effective date and approval.Reporting should be able to represent both. If the system cannot explain why billed value differs from committed value, the team will eventually reconstruct the story from messages. That is a fragile substitute for a maintained evidence trail.Design the cutover around a billing boundaryChoose a specific boundary for the transfer: which periods remain owned by the old system, which begin in the new system, and how straddling amendments will be handled. Document the treatment of open invoices separately from future billing.The plan should identify each account's next expected invoice date, amount basis, responsible system, and collection path. Where exact amounts are not yet known, state why and identify the authoritative calculation source. Do not invent certainty for the sake of a migration checklist.Before enabling new billing, verify that the old system will not independently issue the same obligation. Use supported controls and a reviewed procedure. Do not delete historical records to prevent future activity; history and scheduling are different concerns.If the old system's state cannot be confirmed, stop the affected cohort. A delayed transfer with a named owner is safer than two teams each assuming the other has disabled billing. Preserve the obligation and its due date while resolving the uncertainty.Avoid transferring payment responsibility by assumptionA payment method visible in one system is not proof that another system may use it. Availability, processor support, customer authorization, and migration constraints require separate verification through the approved payment-provider process.Do not export or copy sensitive payment details into spreadsheets, prompts, or ordinary CRM fields. Keep payment operations within approved systems and involve the provider and finance owner for supported transfer paths.Where the payment method cannot move through a supported process, the migration plan may require another collection arrangement. That is a customer-facing and financial decision, not a technical workaround an engineer should invent to complete the import.Similarly, a sandbox demonstration cannot prove that production collection will behave correctly. Define what was tested, what remains unknown, and who must authorize any controlled production verification. No real charge should be initiated merely to make a technical checklist green.A renewal should retain its relationship to the agreement it succeeds. Otherwise the business can count both as active commitments or lose the ability to explain the transition between them.Create fixtures for a standard renewal, an early renewal with changed terms, a renewal while an amendment is pending, a canceled renewal, and an evergreen arrangement. Define which dates, values, and associations should be visible at each stage.Do not assume that every agreement has a meaningful end date. A finite-term test suite is not enough to validate an evergreen population. Segment the migration by commercial shape and verify each supported path separately.Also test the downstream account view. Customer success should be able to distinguish current entitlement from a proposed future package. Sales should see the renewal opportunity without interpreting it as already committed. Finance should retain the link between issued documents and the agreement revision that produced them.Recover forward with evidenceA rollback plan should state what can be reversed and what cannot. A draft record may be editable. An invoice already delivered or a payment already collected may require a formal correction process rather than deletion.Prepare an exception queue for duplicate schedules, missing associations, uncertain collection outcomes, mismatched terms, and unprocessed changes. Each exception needs an owner, a containment action, and a verification requirement.If a timeout leaves the outcome of a consequential operation uncertain, inspect the owning system before repeating the operation. Retrying a read is different from retrying a create or charge. A migration tool should reflect that difference in its recovery procedure.Keep a cutover journal with the cohort, checkpoint, decisions, verification evidence, and unresolved items. It need not be elaborate. It must remain usable when the engineer who performed the migration is unavailable and another person needs to explain the next bill.Make the exit criteria about responsibilityThe migration is ready when the team can answer five questions for every in-scope agreement: what is currently committed, which revision is active, who issues the next invoice, how collection is authorized, and where corrections are recorded.Verify those answers after an amendment and a renewal, not only after the first import. Reconcile a sample forward from agreement to bill and backward from bill to approved terms.Revenue Hub's newer contract capabilities expand the options for connecting commercial history with customer context. The implementation succeeds when those options produce one clear responsibility for the next obligation. A populated contract record is useful. A defensible billing handoff is the actual cutover.Documentation checked October 20, 2026. This article proposes technical controls and does not provide accounting, legal, payment-provider, or tax advice. Verify beta eligibility and supported migration behavior in the relevant account.

item.title: Marvel's Wolverine Sells 2.4 Million Units: Is This Good or Bad?
item.author: Jose
item.content:encoded: Just a few months ago, Marvel’s Wolverine was released to mixed reception. Some people thought the game was pretty good, while others thought that it was everything wrong with AAA gaming. But regardless of how they felt about it, a lot of people assumed that it didn’t matter if reception was mixed; the game was going to sell well anyways. Even I was on board this thought train. Well, as it turns out, that’s not really the case.During Sony’s Q2 FY2026 Consolidated Financial Results speech, it was revealed that Marvel’s Wolverine sold 2.4 million units. Nowhere in the speech does it say that the company is disappointed with this number or that they were expecting it to be much higher. However, by just comparing it to the company’s previous titles, it’s obvious that this number is not in the same ballpark.I compared it to previous Sony games. Take a look:I couldn’t figure out how many units Marvel’s Spider-Man: Miles Morales sold within the first 50 days of its launch, or else I would’ve put it here. But let’s take a look at the other 3 games. Wolverine is trailing behind all three.Although Ghost of Yotei is the highly anticipated sequel to a beloved game, I would’ve thought that Marvel and Wolverine’s brand recognition would’ve allowed it to surpass it. Then, we have to compare it to its predecessors, the Spider-Man games. I think most people would agree that Spider-Man is more well-known than Wolverine, but it’s not like he’s a C-list character or anything. It’s not surprising that Spidey’s games sold better, but it’s surprising that they sold way, way better.By all counts, Marvel’s Wolverine should’ve been a smash hit. It was made by a studio that has developed a reputation as being video game adaptation studio. They had 3 great-selling games, with each game having a positive reception with fans and critics alike. Spider-Man 2 less so than the others, but at the time of its release, that game was being praised to the high heavens.So, what happened? I think word of mouth killed the momentum of this game. Sure, the critics were mixed about it, but a lot of people choose to ignore reviews. However, what was really hurtful to the game’s reputation was what people were saying about it online. Those who’ve played it hated the story, repetitive gameplay, and the over-the-top hand-holding. Most importantly, I think a lot of people were just tired of PlayStation’s “cinematic game” formula. And unfortunately, for Marvel’s Wolverine, it was released at the wrong time.Okay. We’ve looked at the game’s sales, compared it to similar titles, and talked about why it didn’t sell as much as it probably should’ve. We haven’t talked about the most important thing, though. Is 2.4 million units sold a good number for Marvel’s Wolverine?The answer is: There’s no way this met sales expectations. When the studio’s previous games did way better in an even shorter timeframe, Wolverine’s sales can only be seen as disappointing. Nobody is saying that this game is a colossal flop and that Insomniac Games will shut down by the end of the year, but it’s safe to say that this game wasn’t the home run that Sony expected.So, where do we go from here? Hopefully, Insomniac Games and PlayStation listen to the feedback and realize that the formula has to change. Fans have made it loud and clear that what worked 10 years ago won’t work now. I, for one, have faith that they can regroup and come back stronger for their next game.

item.title: Mexico's Senate Approves ISP Rules To Disconnect Persistent Online Pirates
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: On Tuesday, Mexico's Senate approved (PDF) a reform of the Federal Copyright Law that ties ISP liability to having a policy to terminate repeat infringers. [This policy has to be published permanently on their website and in their terms of service, and it must include a basic way to notify users. In other words, what can be terminated is the Internet connection itself, not just an account. According to Mexican business outlet EL CEO, this means that access providers such as Telmex and Izzi will need such a policy.] The Senate approved the amendments with roughly two-thirds of the vote, as the opposition voted against. The Chamber of Deputies already approved the same text in October, so the decree now goes to President Claudia Sheinbaum. Her government proposed the changes in May to bring the law in line with the USMCA trade agreement between Mexico, the United States and Canada.
[...] Providers that don't comply risk facing liability. Under the new rules, any ISP that fails to meet its safe harbor conditions becomes liable for its users' infringements if it knowingly contributes to, induces, or causes the infringement. The same goes for an ISP that can control the infringing user and profits directly from the infringement. In both cases, the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI) can fine the provider up to roughly 4.7 million pesos (~$250,000), depending on the infringement. The law doesn't explicitly define the term repeat infringer, nor does it say how many piracy accusations it takes before a subscriber can be cut off. According to Aurora Lopez-Portillo, director of legal services at IP firm ClarkeModet, each provider has to decide its own threshold. She told EL CEO that ISPs should also check whether the accusations actually hold up, while giving users a chance to respond, even though the law doesn't require that.
During Tuesday's Senate debate, some lawmakers in the opposition raised similar concerns. Senator Gabriel Elizondo warned that families can share a single connection, so the pirating activities of one person could leave an entire household offline. Previously, opposition lawmakers proposed requiring a court order before Internet service could be suspended, but that proposal was not adopted. [...] There, failing to meet the safe harbor conditions, including the repeat infringer policy, is the first requirement for liability. If an ISP also contributes to infringement with knowledge of it, or can control the infringer and directly profits from it, it can be held responsible. The new repeat infringer rules will take effect 180 days after their publication in Mexico's official gazette, which hasn't happened yet as far as we can see. How Mexican ISPs will define a repeat infringer, and how many accusations it takes, has yet to be seen.

item.title: 104 Blog Posts To Learn About Problem Solving

item.content:encoded: Let's learn about Problem Solving via these 104 free blog posts. They are ordered by HackerNoon reader engagement data. Visit the Learn Repo or LearnRepo.com to find the most read blog posts about any technology.Problem-solving is the process of identifying a problem, generating potential solutions, evaluating them, and implementing the most effective one. It is a fundamental skill in all aspects of technology and life, driving innovation and efficiency across various domains. Given an array, the algorithm to find the maximum subarray sum is called Kadane’s Algorithm. There is no programmer in the world who knows how to solve every coding problem. That person simply doesn’t exist, because the programming field is so big that to a normal person, it would take two lives to learn all of that, but we only have one life. Manacher’s Algorithm helps us find the longest palindromic substring in the given string. It optimizes over the brute force solution by using some insights into how palindromes work. How? Let’s see! System thinking is a valuable framework for generalists, you need a proper framework for organizing your multiple thoughts, passions, and pursuits. Julia MacDonald, a Fractional Growth Executive, breaks down a 7-step framework to solve any problem. Merrill's First Principles of Instruction are a series of very effective problem-based teaching methodologies. The principles are based on the five core princip I find the Monty Hall Problem one of the most fascinating brain teasers, because it seems deceivingly simple. When Marilyn Von Savant, the woman with the highest IQ, answered this brainteaser correctly in 1991, she was inundated with over 10,000 letters from academics and Ph.Ds criticizing her “error”, only to be proven later that she was correct. TL, DR; When coming across an ML problem, don’t try to be a hero and dive right into solving it. Process and understand the problem, review your dataset, set a realistic goal and then go about actually solving the problem. Chances are that you will end up saving a lot of resources (most importantly time) if you plan your execution properly. What does it mean to be a generalist? If you are one, how can you find purpose and thrive in your life? We'll answer these questions and more in this articl The first question that arises when solving a problem using dynamic programming(DP) is how to figure out that DP is a way to solve it? Have you ever written a program for pairing alternate positive and negative numbers? If not, then you are missing some great opportunities.
