item.title: SpaceX Teams Up With Qualcomm to Build a Nationwide 5G Network
item.author: Bruce Li
item.content:encoded: The company that put thousands of routers in orbit is now coming down to earth: steel towers, rooftop leases, zoning boards and all. Here's what's planned, how 5G works, and why the hard part isn't the rockets.Back in February 2020, I wrote a parody called "SpaceX Starlink Master Plan", in the voice of a certain CEO. It copied the "trickle-down" structure of Tesla's master plan, in four steps:Build a bulky, expensive terminal for professionals.Use that money to build a rooftop consumer terminal.Use that money to build "a low cost and high volume mobile phone."Build an interstellar communication system for Mars and beyond.Fake-Elon also bragged that Starlink could beat 5G because the carriers "need to deploy a lot more cell sites," while Starlink doesn't "need to pay site rentals and backhaul." For the astronomers, he promised to paint every satellite chroma green "so they can be easily removed in photoshop."Six and a half years later, steps 1 and 2 happened, if not quite in that order (consumers came first): millions of pizza-box dishes, on roofs and on boats. Step 3 took a turn I didn't see coming. SpaceX never built a StarPhone; it made phone a StarPhone, beaming signals straight to the one already in your pocket. And now comes the twist the parody never imagined: SpaceX is about to pay site rentals. Lots of them.For about 30 years, American mobile service has worked like this: three giant companies own the networks (the airwaves, the radios bolted to the towers, and your monthly bill), and everyone else rents from them. Not even the giants own most of the towers anymore. Over a decade ago they sold or long-term leased them to landlords like American Tower and Crown Castle, and now pay rent like everybody else. Upstarts have tried to break in. Most have ended up as footnotes, or as a Boost Mobile ad.Now a rocket company wants a go. On November 4, 2026, SpaceX and Qualcomm announced a multi-year deal under which Qualcomm supplies the core radio silicon and software for a nationwide terrestrial 5G network under the Starlink Mobile brand. SpaceX already has phone service coming from orbit. This time the plan is phone service coming , from tens of thousands of ordinary cell sites. Construction starts in 2027; when you can actually get service from them, nobody has said.So: what exactly was announced, how does the technology work, and how many billions of dollars and zoning hearings stand between SpaceX and your SIM card?1. The Announcement: Starlink Gets a Ground GameQualcomm supplies the guts of the radio access network (RAN): the radio-unit and baseband platforms (chips plus reference designs) and the commercial-grade Layer 1 software, all from its cellular infrastructure line. SpaceX builds the actual boxes around them. Neither company disclosed the dollar value. "Tens of thousands of sites," according to the announcement, and Qualcomm executive vice president Durga Malladi expects the rollout to "ramp up pretty rapidly." Unconfirmed press reports say SpaceX is talking to tower owners about access to as many as ; no tower partners have been named. Tower deployment starts in 2027. No launch date for terrestrial service has been given. Separately, SpaceX is targeting to switch on its next-generation "full 5G quality" service. a genuine fourth national carrier that owns its own network, not just another reseller.Malladi called it "huge," and agreed with Light Reading that it's Qualcomm's biggest network deal since 3G. For a company best known for the modem in your phone, that's a big deal.Dragonwing, launched in February 2025, is Qualcomm's brand for its industrial, networking and infrastructure silicon, the chips that go into things other than phones.The Dragonwing toolbox (the deal announcement names the QRU100 and QDU100 platforms specifically):Radio unit platform supporting massive MIMO (64 transmit, 64 receive paths)Up on the tower, behind the antennaDistributed-unit Layer 1 baseband platform; its card form, the X100, is an inline PCIe accelerator (35 W max) that slots into ordinary Dell or HPE serversIn a cabinet at the base of the tower or a nearby edge siteThe RF transceiver chips that turn bits into radio waves and backAI features + RAN Automation SuiteAI beam prediction, uplink tuning and factory calibration built into the platforms, plus a separate network-management suiteEverywhere, apparently, because it's 2026This gear has been deployed before, though not at this scale. Vietnam's runs Qualcomm-based radios across "a few thousand sites," and Qualcomm chips have shown up inside radios from NEC and Mavenir (which has since quit making radios). SpaceX is about to become its first customer at continental scale.Qualcomm handles the physical layer, the hard real-time signal math. SpaceX is expected to write its own Layer 2, Layer 3 and core network software on top. As Malladi put it, "They still have to do the Layer 2, the Layer 3, and so on." That's very SpaceX: buy the chips and own the software, the same way it treats rocket engines and satellite buses.The airwaves SpaceX has lined upRadios are useless without airwaves, and in about 13 months SpaceX has agreed to spend roughly on spectrum (not all of it paid yet):EchoStar (September 2025): about 50 MHz of 2 GHz AWS-4 and H-Block spectrum for about $17 billion (half cash, half SpaceX stock), plus roughly $2 billion of EchoStar's debt interest. In November 2025 SpaceX added a 15 MHz uplink-only AWS-3 slice (1695–1710 MHz) for about $2.6 billion in stock, for a total of roughly . The FCC approved the deal in May 2026 and allowed the spectrum to be used from space, on the ground, or both, which SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen calls crucial. The final closing, when SpaceX actually pays, is expected around late 2027.Grain Management (October 2026): up to 14 MHz of paired, nationwide low-band spectrum for a reported (terms undisclosed; FCC approval pending). These airwaves started life at Nextel, passed to Sprint and then T-Mobile, which sold them to private investor Grain for about $3.6 billion ($2.9 billion in cash plus Grain's 600 MHz licenses) in a deal that closed in August 2026. Grain flipped them to SpaceX two months later for more than double that, which suggests either very good timing or a buyer in a hurry.SpaceX is also reportedly (per the ) in talks to buy from EchoStar. That would bring an existing customer base, retail distribution, and wholesale roaming deals with AT&T and T-Mobile, two carriers that have so far shown little interest in signing anything directly with Elon Musk.2. The State of American Wireless: Three Giants and a Rounding ErrorThe U.S. market is a mature three-way oligopoly. Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile together serve the overwhelming majority of American phone lines, each with roughly 120 to 147 million connections. Cable companies (Comcast's Xfinity Mobile, Charter's Spectrum Mobile, about 23 million lines combined) have become the fastest-growing challengers, but they cheat a little: their consumer service runs on Verizon's network as an MVNO, and they push as much traffic as possible onto their own Wi-Fi (plus some CBRS small cells). the 5G speed leader, thanks to Sprint's mid-band spectrum. It holds "nearly 400 MHz" of airwaves. Remember that number. the coverage champ, finally growing again (406,000 postpaid phone adds in Q3 2026). betting on fiber-plus-wireless bundles, and swapping its Nokia gear for Ericsson's.AT&T and Verizon each plan to spend $16–24 billion on their networks in 2026, and T-Mobile about $10 billion. That's the annual fee for staying in this business.Pay more, get… about the sameA three-way oligopoly is a comfortable place to be, if you're one of the three. Americans pay some of the highest mobile prices in the developed world:Avg. mobile revenue per user, per month (2023)Major mobile network operatorsTypically 3–4 per countrySource: Connect Europe, State of Digital Communications 2025.Notably, South Korea also has just three carriers and still charges far less, so the number of players isn't the whole story. Scale, geography and decades of regulatory choices all play a part.That pricing turns into money. The Big Three post EBITDA margins in the mid-30s percent, which makes them some of the most profitable mobile operators anywhere. European carriers, squeezed by cutthroat competition, have spent the past decade complaining about the opposite problem.What do Americans get for the premium? A good network, but not a world-beating one. Opensignal's Global Network Excellence Index ranked the U.S. in the world in late 2025, behind South Korea, among others. Ookla's Speedtest index has put U.S. median mobile download speeds somewhere between 9th and 13th in recent months, far behind the Gulf states and South Korea. And the rural dead zones are still there. In fairness, covering a huge, sparsely populated continent costs more than wiring Seoul. But that gap between price and performance is exactly the opening a fourth carrier is looking for.The cautionary tale named DishThe last company to try building a fourth facilities-based network was Dish (later EchoStar). Regulators made it the designated fourth carrier as a condition of the T-Mobile–Sprint merger, which closed in 2020. It built what it billed as the world's first cloud-native Open RAN 5G network and hit its 2023 coverage milestone of 70% of the population (its later deadline was pushed back). Then in 2025 it agreed to sell its spectrum to AT&T and SpaceX, and it is now moving Boost customers onto AT&T's network as a hybrid MVNO. Its wireless unit filed for Chapter 11 in mid-2026.So the most recent attempt to build a new U.S. carrier ended with a handful of companies dividing up its airwaves, and SpaceX was one of the buyers.Where Starlink 5G could fitSpaceX isn't going to out-Verizon Verizon in midtown Manhattan in 2028. It's going after the problems the incumbents have never fully solved: Highways through the Mojave, national parks, farmland, the stretch of interstate where your podcast always cuts out. The carriers' coverage maps are generous, and the reality is patchier. Towers rarely pay for themselves out there; SpaceX's satellites can cover those gaps without them.Seamless ground-to-space handoff. Today, satellite texting from T-Mobile's T-Satellite or Apple's Globalstar-based service (Amazon is buying Globalstar) is a separate, slower mode you drop into. SpaceX wants a single network where your phone moves from tower to satellite and back without you noticing. Starlink already rattled the broadband market. A carrier with no legacy network and no union-negotiated copper plant to maintain could undercut the incumbents on price, or charge a premium for "never lose signal."The incumbents, for their part, sound unbothered. "The physics just don't allow direct-to-cell to be a substitute product," said T-Mobile's (outgoing) CFO Peter Osvaldik in September. Verizon CEO Dan Schulman said Starlink "just can't compete without a terrestrial network in urban and suburban." Hence the towers.3. A Primer on Cellular, 5G, and Phones That Talk to SpaceCellular in one paragraphA cellular network divides the world into , areas each served by a base station. Your phone talks to the nearest one over licensed radio spectrum. The base station passes your data back over (fiber, or a microwave radio link) to the operator's , which handles authentication, billing, mobility, and the connection to the internet. When you move, the network hands you off to the next cell. Every generation since the 1980s (1G analog voice, 2G digital voice and SMS, 3G mobile data, 4G LTE mobile broadband, 5G) has been a better trick for packing more bits into the same air.What actually makes 5G faster5G New Radio (NR) isn't magic. It uses three broad levers:1. More spectrum, in three flavors. Radio physics forces a trade-off: lower frequencies travel farther and go through walls, while higher frequencies carry more data but give up at the first pane of low-E glass. the coverage layer. Goes for miles and works deep indoors. Spectrum is scarce, so channels are narrow. SpaceX's 800 MHz lives here.Mid-band (roughly 1–7 GHz): the "Goldilocks" layer, a usable mix of reach and capacity. This is where 5G mostly lives. SpaceX's 2 GHz AWS-4 lives here.High-band / mmWave (24 GHz+): blazing fast, with a range of about a city block, and blocked by leaves, rain, and your own hand. Mostly found in stadiums and press releases. Every radio symbol encodes bits through combinations of amplitude and phase. Since 3GPP Release 17, 5G's downlink supports up to , meaning 10 bits per symbol, but only when the signal is clean enough. It's like a crowded restaurant: the quieter the room, the faster you can talk.3. Massive MIMO and beamforming. This is the big one. An old 4G antenna is a floodlight: it sprays energy across a whole 120° sector. A 5G panel such as Qualcomm's 64T64R has dozens of small antenna elements. By adjusting the phase of each element's signal, the base station makes the waves add up in some directions and cancel in others. That produces focused aimed at individual phones.Once you can aim beams, you can reuse the same frequencies for several users at the same time, as long as they're in different places. This is . Vendor and industry estimates suggest a 64T64R sector can carry roughly of a 4T4R sector on the same 100 MHz, and give users at the cell edge a signal boost of around 9 dB.There's a catch that matters a lot for SpaceX. Most massive MIMO deployments use spectrum, where uplink and downlink take turns on the same channel, which makes it easy for the base station to learn the radio channel. SpaceX's spectrum is all : paired blocks with separate uplink and downlink channels, plus an uplink-only slice, and no TDD at all. Massive MIMO is harder to do well on FDD, and the FDD deployments out there today are mostly 32T32R. "If they're spectrum constrained, which they are, then this FDD massive MIMO is the way to get the capacity but especially the coverage benefits," says Omdia analyst Gabriel Brown. Qualcomm's pitch is that it can make 64T64R work well on SpaceX's 2 GHz FDD bands. A lot depends on that being true.Plus the 5G stuff you've heard about. A standalone 5G core makes possible (virtual private networks with guaranteed performance), lower latency, and better handling of huge numbers of IoT devices. These matter for enterprises and are mostly invisible to people scrolling TikTok.Now contrast that with a cell tower in orbitSpaceX's existing satellites (about 650 launched since January 2024) work on a seemingly impossible premise: talk to an smartphone from hundreds of kilometers up.Here is what they're up against:~350–550 km (and more at an angle)Still ~0.2 W. Your phone didn't get strongerA beam tens of kilometers widePotentially thousands (illustrative)Mostly no; you need sky viewNone; the tower stays putSatellite moves at ~7.6 km/s and the network must handle Doppler shift and constant handoffsTexts, low-rate data, some appsThe satellites make up for it with brute force: huge phased-array antennas (several square meters) and very sensitive receivers, so they can pick up a phone's faint signal from orbit. Each satellite is essentially an eNodeB (an LTE base station) in space, backhauled through laser links to the rest of Starlink. That's the clever part. The phone thinks it's talking to an unusually distant tower in a roaming partner's network.SpaceX's next-generation satellites, dubbed Starlink Mobile V2 and borrowing technology from its V3 broadband satellites, start launching on Starship around mid-2027. In October 2026 the FCC authorized a constellation of up to 15,000 of them. CFO Johnsen promises a "full 5G quality service," and SpaceX's target is up to 150 Mbps per user at peak. New 3GPP Release 19 phone modems with built-in satellite support, like Qualcomm's X105, should help. Even so, physics has a vote. A satellite beam covering a whole county is one shared cell. It will never match the capacity of a dense mesh of towers in a city.That's the whole logic of the terrestrial plan: towers for capacity, satellites for coverage, one network for both.The traditional cartel… er, "ecosystem"Global RAN equipment is one of the most concentrated markets in tech. According to Dell'Oro and Omdia, the top five vendors (Huawei, Ericsson, Nokia, ZTE and Samsung) took about 95–96% of RAN revenue in 2025, and Dell'Oro says market concentration hit a ten-year high. the global #1. Together with Ericsson, it holds nearly two-thirds of the market. Huawei is also banned from U.S. networks for national security reasons, and rural carriers are still working through a federally funded "rip and replace" program to remove its gear (fully funded since 2025, about half done). the U.S. heavyweight, with more than 60% of North American RAN. In December 2023 it won AT&T's Open RAN contract, worth up to $14 billion. Ericsson is the vendor you hire when you want nobody to get fired. #3 globally, T-Mobile's other main RAN supplier, which lost AT&T to Ericsson. It got a lifeline from NVIDIA in October 2025: a $1 billion investment to develop GPU-based "AI-RAN." the other Chinese giant, also effectively shut out of the U.S. the top challenger in the U.S., with a $6.6 billion Verizon contract and virtualized RAN software that runs on standard servers. It also supplied part of Dish's network.The traditional model was : the radio on the tower and the baseband box at the bottom came from the same vendor and spoke a proprietary dialect over the cable between them. Once you'd picked Ericsson, you were an Ericsson shop for a decade.Open RAN cracks the box open (driven by the O-RAN Alliance) standardizes the interfaces inside the base station so operators can mix vendors. It splits the base station into three parts: on the tower. Antennas, amplifiers, the lowest-level signal processing. an ordinary server near the tower doing real-time baseband work: scheduling, error correction, beamforming math. software in a data center or cloud handling the less time-critical protocol layers.The key standard is the , which defines exactly which signal-processing steps happen in the radio and which happen in the server, connected by plain Ethernet (eCPRI). That standard is the only reason a chip company like Qualcomm can sell what is effectively a full base station design to a carrier like SpaceX without Ericsson in the room. sells : chips and reference designs that radio makers (or ambitious customers) build into products. It is betting on , which runs the entire Layer 1 signal-processing pipeline on a dedicated DSP card (the X100) instead of bouncing data between a general-purpose CPU and an accelerator, the "lookaside" approach Intel long championed (it has since built the accelerator into its Xeon chips). Qualcomm's pitch is cheaper servers, lower power and fewer bottlenecks. The X100 card draws at most 35 W, according to Qualcomm's product brief, and at network scale every watt saved adds up. is pushing on GPUs through its Aerial platform: a cell site that runs the radio and AI inference on the same hardware. Qualcomm's Malladi isn't convinced: "AI-based RAN is a lot more than just throw a GPU at it, and you're done." supply competing baseband silicon, inline and lookaside respectively.Startups and software players: (chiefly a cloud-native core and RAN software vendor, which quit making macro radios in 2025), , (the arm that sells the software behind Rakuten's own Open RAN network in Japan), (Fujitsu's network business, spun out in 2025), and (AI-native signal processing), among others.Open RAN's track record is mixed. Rakuten in Japan and Dish in the U.S. (until EchoStar wound its network down) proved it , though neither proved it . Integrating parts from multiple vendors turned out to be expensive and messy, which is why the radios and baseband in AT&T's "Open RAN" come almost entirely from Ericsson. The first third-party radio, from 1FINITY, only made its first call in 2025. SpaceX is taking a third path: one silicon vendor, its own software, and an engineering culture that would rather build than integrate.5. The Hard Part: Building a National Network From ScratchRockets are hard. Getting a conditional use permit from a county planning board in suburban New Jersey may be harder. Here's what's in the way.Cost: $100 billion, give or take a moon missionEstimates are all over the map. BNP Paribas analyst Sam McHugh reckons SpaceX would need to spend on a terrestrial network before it earns real revenue, . TD Cowen says more than $80 billion, and Bernstein $50–130 billion including spectrum. LightShed thinks the initial build could be as little as $10–15 billion. Verizon's Schulman, who is not a neutral party, says $300–500 billion. Some back-of-envelope numbers show why: SpaceX doesn't own towers. It will lease space from American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA and others; the U.S. has roughly 450,000 cell sites of all kinds. Lease brokers put the ground rent that tower companies pay landowners at around , with urban rooftops at $4,000+. A carrier renting space a tower typically pays more than that, and leases usually rise about 3% a year. Even at a lowball $1,500/month, 50,000 sites comes to before buying a single radio.Equipment and installation. Radios, antennas, servers, power systems, structural analysis, crane time and tower crews. This can run well into six figures for a new site, less for adding gear to an existing one. Electricity at every site, plus a fiber or microwave link to carry its traffic back to the core. Stores, marketing, handset subsidies and customer care. The incumbents spend billions a year on this alone, and most of it is money spent getting people to switch.SpaceX has unusual advantages here: a Starlink broadband business that throws off cash, the ability to raise money at an enormous valuation, and a satellite layer that can cover rural areas, so it doesn't have to build towers everywhere the incumbents did.But deep pockets have a lot of pockets. Since swallowing Elon Musk's xAI in February 2026, SpaceX has been pouring money into AI data centers: capital spending hit a reported $28.5 billion in the first half of 2026, more than triple a year earlier, with most of it going to AI infrastructure such as xAI's Colossus supercomputers in Memphis. Investors knocked the stock down about 13% when that number came out. Every dollar spent on GPUs is a dollar not spent on tower leases. If AI and 5G end up competing for the same budget, it's not obvious the cell towers win.Spectrum: 80 MHz vs. 400 MHzHere's the number from earlier. SpaceX's terrestrial holdings total roughly , and some of that is uplink-only. T-Mobile has nearly . Verizon and AT&T each have hundreds of MHz too, including wide TDD mid-band channels (C-band, 2.5 GHz, 3.45 GHz) that are ideal for massive MIMO.Spectrum is capacity. With a fifth of the airwaves, SpaceX has to squeeze far more out of every MHz, which is why 64T64R FDD massive MIMO and Qualcomm's AI-driven beam prediction are central to the plan and not just marketing. Expect SpaceX to show up at every future FCC auction, starting with the upper C-band auction (160 MHz at 3.98–4.14 GHz), due by July 2027. (An AWS-3 re-auction already wrapped up in June 2026, raising about $3.5 billion.)There's also a band-sharing puzzle: the same 2 GHz spectrum is supposed to serve both towers and satellites. Keeping the two from interfering, especially near the edges of tower coverage where a phone could hear both, takes careful coordination, and it's a novel problem.Time: towers don't launch on StarshipDish took about three years from the Sprint merger to cover roughly 70% of the U.S. population, and it struggled with indoor coverage and actual customer uptake the whole way. The physical rollout is limited by:: thousands of local jurisdictions, each with its own process.: the pool of certified climbers is finite, and the incumbents are already booking them.: a 64T64R massive MIMO radio is heavy and catches a lot of wind. Many tower spots will need reinforcement.: every site needs a fiber or microwave link, and a massive MIMO site moving gigabits needs fiber. Leasing or trenching it, site by site, is slow.Phones: the quiet dependencyYour phone has to support SpaceX's frequencies. The good news is that much of SpaceX's 2 GHz spectrum lines up with 5G (which Dish got into recent phones, iPhones included) and band n66, and the 800 MHz block sits inside band 26, which nearly every U.S. phone supports. One snag: Apple's phones don't list the 4G LTE version of band 70. The less good news: carrier certification, eSIM provisioning, Wi-Fi calling, VoNR voice, emergency-911 location accuracy and roaming agreements are all tedious, unglamorous work, and any one of them can sink a launch. It helps that Qualcomm makes most of the modems in question.AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile are not ignoring the sky. AT&T and Verizon have backed , a direct-to-phone satellite rival. T-Mobile is currently Starlink's own D2C partner, which makes the relationship awkward. In May 2026 the three carriers also agreed to pool spectrum in a joint satellite venture aimed at rural dead zones. SpaceX's CFO reportedly mused that they "wanted to create a cartel, maybe." And they all have one powerful tool: price cuts, funded by networks they paid off years ago.As recently as September 2026, SpaceX's CFO was publicly hedging on whether it would build a terrestrial network at all, keeping options open for an MVNO arrangement or rooftop "femtocells" next to Starlink dishes. The Qualcomm deal suggests the company has made up its mind. Still, signing a supply contract is the easy part.6. Milestones to Watch, 2026–2036Near term (2026–2027): Paper and steelFCC filings and master lease agreements. How many sites, which markets first, and with which tower companies. Watch for an American Tower or Crown Castle master lease announcement. It would be the first hard evidence of real scale.Boost Mobile acquisition. If it closes, SpaceX gets millions of customers and a roaming bridge on day one.Starlink Mobile V2 satellites on Starship (from mid-2027). These next-generation satellites carry the "full 5G" satellite layer. Each Starship launch matters.EchoStar closing (around late 2027) and FCC approval of the Grain 800 MHz deal.First cell sites go up (2027). Watch where the first clusters appear, and for any trial service. When drive-test data shows up on Ookla or Opensignal, the network is real.Medium term (2028–2030): Show me the subscribers The satellite 5G service is targeted for early 2028; watch for the terrestrial launch date. Pricing will tell you the strategy: aggressive undercutting or a premium "never offline" tier., especially iPhone. If Apple certifies a carrier, that carrier is real.Population coverage claims vs. reality. Can SpaceX reach 50%+ of the population with good service? This is where Dish struggled.Subscriber numbers and churn. In wireless, adding customers gets the headlines, but keeping them is what makes the money. The upper C-band auction (2027), or more secondary-market deals.Long term (2030–2036): The 6G turn6G standards (3GPP Release 21, ~2028–2029) and first 6G deployments (~2030). Satellite links are being designed into 6G from the start, which plays to SpaceX's strengths. Qualcomm is already floating a "giga-MIMO" concept with 128 or 256 transmitters and receivers per radio, and Malladi says the deal will "lay the foundation for AI-native 6G." The end goal is a single core network, one phone number, and handoffs between tower and satellite that nobody notices. If SpaceX gets there first, the dead zone stops being a fact of life and becomes a product choice.The market structure question. By the mid-2030s, either the U.S. has a durable fourth carrier with its own satellites, or there's one more company dividing up a former challenger's spectrum. There's not much middle ground.SpaceX is doing something no operator has tried: building a cellular network from the sky down, with satellites for coverage, towers for capacity, and Qualcomm silicon to make the towers cheap and power-efficient enough to deploy by the tens of thousands.The technology is plausible. The spectrum is thin but usable. The money exists, at least for SpaceX. What remains is the unglamorous work that has humbled every challenger before it: leases, permits, crews, phone certification, customer care and price wars.SpaceX has a habit of turning "impossible" into "late, but done." Phone networks are a slower industry, measured in zoning variances instead of launch windows. Either way, the next few years will be interesting, and probably good news for anyone's phone bill.Even if SpaceX stumbles, the industry is better off for the attempt. In 2023 I wrote an obituary, "R.I.P. 'Innovation in Mobile' (2015–2023)", blaming three killers: mergers that wiped out independent carriers, the big three swallowing the MVNOs, and spectrum priced beyond any challenger's reach. SpaceX is taking on all three. It has committed roughly $28 billion to spectrum, and, shut out as an MVNO, it is building its own network as an independent carrier. Even if it never wins, it forces everyone else to move. Maybe the obituary was premature.In my 2020 parody, fake-Elon bragged about never paying for cell sites or backhaul. Real SpaceX is about to pay for both, which is the most grown-up thing a rocket company has ever done. Master plan amendment, Step 3b: If it works, your next dead zone might just be a fond memory.The chroma-green satellites are still pending. Don't tell anyone.

item.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Summoned By Congress Over Chinese Espionage Concerns
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Top Republican lawmakers have asked Jensen Huang to appear before Congress to answer questions after it was reported that US intelligence officials believe Nvidia's chief executive has been targeted by a Chinese spying operation. The chairs of the House committees on China, foreign affairs, and intelligence wrote to Huang this week asking him to appear before a joint closed-door briefing for their committees on November 18. "Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the People's Republic of China's access to sensitive US technology and information," representatives John Moolenaar, Brian Mast, and Rick Crawford wrote. "The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk," the lawmakers added.
The New York Times last week wrote that US intelligence officials believed Huang had been the target of a Chinese spy operation. The concerns center on a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company that has bought billions of dollars of Nvidia's chips. Nvidia has rejected the claims and on Thursday would not say if Huang would appear before Congress. "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job. Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," the company said. "Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information -- not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets -- and zero information relevant to national security," it added.
The lawmakers said they wanted Huang to discuss the security protocols Nvidia had in place to protect against "foreign adversary espionage." The company said its chief executive had an "outstanding security team" that travels with him. The New York Times said Huang had not received a "defensive briefing," which the intelligence community usually, but not always, provides potential espionage targets to warn them about the activity. Nvidia said it was confident that the US government would have let the company know if it thought a person was a threat to US industry and that it often receives updates from Washington about people of concern.

item.title: 18 Agent Skills Design Frontends, Brands and Themes With Real Taste
item.author: Iconography Technology
item.content:encoded: Eighteen open-licensed agent skills give an AI agent design judgment: distinctive frontends, brand-consistent themes, Figma-to-code translation, accessibility audits, SwiftUI patterns and generative art. Seven come from Anthropic, including its frontend-design skill. Nine come from Tech Leads Club, and Matt Pocock and Thomas Ricouard contribute one each.Creates generative art in p5.js with seeded randomness and tunable parametersApplies Anthropic's brand colors and typography; a template for encoding your own brandCreates visual art as PNG and PDF from a design philosophyShared vocabulary for designing deep modules and clean interfacesPulls design context, variables and assets from Figma through its MCP serverRuns a design discovery process before generating any frontend codeBrings distinctive, intentional visual design to new or existing UIBuilds production-grade frontends with high design qualityDesigns new skills through a structured conversationExample-driven patterns for SwiftUI views, navigation and modifiersApplies ready-made or custom themes to slides, docs and pages/plugin marketplace add hackernoon/cuttlefish-agent-skills /plugin install design-ui@cuttlefish For Codex CLI, Cursor or another agent that supports the standard, clone the repo and copy plugins/design-ui/skills/ into your agent's skills folder, such as . The two frontend-design skills install under different folder names, so both can sit side by side.

item.title: Will Open-Source Software Survive the AI Vulnerability Flood?
item.author: Sebastian Martinez Torregrosa
item.content:encoded: Why the AI-driven vulnerability flood could hit open-source maintainers harder today—and leave surviving projects more secure tomorrow.We may be entering the largest vulnerability discovery wave in software history. AI is making it practical to examine billions of lines of legacy code more thoroughly and continuously, reassessing their security as they interact with new components and environments. One potential consequence is a sharp increase in reported vulnerabilities, and some projects are already experiencing the pressure.But open source appears to be facing this wave earlier and more visibly than closed source. Does that mean proprietary software is more secure in the age of AI?And can open-source projects survive the flood?The more interesting question is what happens after it.Software complexity makes vulnerability discovery a universal challenge. Vulnerabilities can emerge from interactions between components, dependencies, and changing environments—even when the underlying code has not changed. Continuous security reassessment, using evolving AI capabilities, is essential across both open- and closed-source software.The AI-driven vulnerability flood will be a temporary peak, not permanent growth. AI-assisted analysis will progressively deplete the finite backlog of detectable historical vulnerabilities, while continuous security analysis in development and CI/CD will reduce its replenishment. Vulnerability discovery will continue, but at a lower rate once the initial backlog has been substantially examined.Open-source projects may face the flood before they can adapt. Easier access to source code and broader independent scrutiny could accelerate vulnerability discovery, overwhelming individual maintainers and communities whose security-response capacity cannot scale quickly enough.Open-source software could become more secure, but its ecosystem will face growing pressure to reorganize. AI-driven vulnerability discovery and growing security obligations could expose the longstanding fragility of critical dependencies maintained by small, underfunded communities. The resulting pressure may accelerate funding changes, consolidation, and project abandonment—potentially producing more secure surviving projects, but a less diverse ecosystem with new concentrations of systemic risk.Closed source is not necessarily safer—it may simply face the flood later. Restricted access to code and binaries can delay independent discovery and reduce public visibility, potentially leaving historical vulnerabilities undiscovered and unfixed for longer. Internal vendor analysis can alter this trajectory.More public vulnerabilities today could mean fewer exploitable vulnerabilities tomorrow. Broad AI-assisted scrutiny of open-source code may accelerate the discovery and elimination of historical vulnerabilities. Closed-source software may retain a larger hidden backlog for longer, while attackers can independently discover and exploit vulnerabilities regardless of public disclosure. Higher CVE counts may therefore reflect faster elimination of hidden risks, not inherently less secure software.Enterprises must accelerate remediation from patch creation to production. AI compresses the discovery-to-exploitation window, making traditional patch deployment timelines increasingly dangerous. Automated testing, cloud-native rolling updates, user-space live patching, and high-availability clustering can reduce deployment delays without sacrificing service continuity.Every mature codebase carries an unknown number of undiscovered vulnerabilities. Some were introduced recently. Many have existed for years or decades.Traditional security research was always constrained by human time and expertise, so the number of vulnerabilities reported was never a reliable measure of the number that existed.A project with ten CVEs was not necessarily less secure than one with none; it may simply have been examined more carefully.AI changes the economics of that examination. Analysis that once required sustained expert attention can increasingly be automated, repeated, and applied across large codebases.Historically, discovering or disclosing a vulnerability did not necessarily make it immediately exploitable at scale. Some vulnerabilities may already have been exploited privately as zero-days for years before public discovery or disclosure. Developing a reliable exploit often required specialized expertise and considerable time. AI is eroding that barrier. It can accelerate exploit development, automate parts of the exploitation process, and make sophisticated attacks accessible to a much broader range of attackers. The interval between vulnerability discovery and widespread exploitation could shrink dramatically, potentially approaching zero for some classes of vulnerabilities.The more intensively software is examined, the worse its reported security can initially appear—not because the code has changed, but because previously invisible defects are becoming visible.A Temporary Peak, Not a Permanent ElevationFor relatively stable codebases, the result should be a temporary peak in vulnerability discovery rather than a permanently elevated discovery rate.AI-assisted analysis first encounters the accumulated backlog. Discoveries accelerate. Mature projects that reported relatively few issues may suddenly generate substantial numbers.As detectable legacy flaws are progressively discovered, the remaining backlog of undiscovered vulnerabilities should eventually shrink. Whether the software actually becomes safer depends on how quickly those discoveries are converted into effective fixes.The prediction is that the initial discovery flood will be temporary, not that vulnerability discovery will eventually stop. Its timing, magnitude, and duration will differ across projects, languages, and ecosystems.A similar possibility was raised by, which suggested that AI-driven vulnerability discovery could eventually exhaust much of the readily discoverable historical backlog, while AI-assisted security testing during development could help reduce future vulnerability accumulation.Software continues to change. New features, dependencies, architectural shifts, and AI-generated code can introduce fresh vulnerabilities. Even unchanged legacy code may become exploitable when combined with new components or exposed in different environments. Vulnerabilities can also emerge from interactions between individually secure components, making security a property of the integrated system, not just its individual parts. This makes continuous reassessment necessary across both open- and closed-source software, not merely repeated analysis of newly written code.Continuous reassessment must also evolve with AI itself. As AI analysis improves, it may identify vulnerability classes, attack paths, and complex interactions that earlier generations of tools could not detect—even in code that has not changed. A completed security scan therefore represents an assessment using the capabilities available at that time, not a permanent declaration that the software is secure.The historical backlog accumulated over decades when comprehensive security analysis was expensive and largely dependent on human expertise. New software will increasingly be developed under very different conditions.As AI-assisted vulnerability detection becomes integrated into CI/CD pipelines, newly written code can be examined continuously, allowing vulnerabilities to be discovered and corrected before they reach production or accumulate into another historical backlog.For this reduction to be sustainable, AI-assisted vulnerability detection must eventually become a commodity: an affordable, routine part of software development rather than an expensive, separately commissioned security activity. Finding and fixing vulnerabilities while code is still being written is far cheaper than discovering them years after deployment, when remediation may require coordinated disclosure, backports, and production patching.This security analysis must also remain distinct from AI-assisted code generation. Both can coexist in the same development workflow, but generating code and independently evaluating its security are different responsibilities. Vulnerability detection requires dedicated security-focused tools and AI systems trained or optimized for that purpose. Just as compilation does not replace testing, an AI system that produces code should not be relied upon as its sole security reviewer.AI therefore creates two opposing pressures on vulnerability accumulation. AI-assisted coding can accelerate the introduction of new vulnerabilities as software production scales, potentially sustaining elevated discovery rates even after much of the historical backlog has been examined. Continuous, independent AI-assisted security analysis during development can counteract that effect by identifying and correcting vulnerabilities before they reach production. Without that second mechanism, the predicted decline in vulnerability discovery rates may never materialize.Not every defect will be detected. But the most readily detectable vulnerabilities should increasingly be identified and eliminated during development rather than accumulating unnoticed for years.This creates two complementary mechanisms: AI-driven discovery and remediation reduce the historical vulnerability backlog, while continuous AI-assisted security analysis limits its replenishment.AI-assisted vulnerability detection should therefore become a continuous, standard part of CI/CD pipelines, rather than an occasional security assessment.AI detection capabilities will continue improving, but their effectiveness need not grow exponentially forever. As techniques mature and become widely adopted, the most readily detectable vulnerabilities should become progressively less common in both legacy and newly developed code.The expected outcome is therefore an initial discovery flood followed by a smaller, continuous flow of newly discovered vulnerabilities—not the disappearance of vulnerabilities altogether.New vulnerability classes, major architectural changes, and uneven adoption could produce further discovery waves. But they do not necessarily imply that the enormous historical backlog can be recreated at the same rate.A lasting reduction in the total vulnerability stock requires effective elimination to exceed the introduction of new vulnerabilities.Discovery enables elimination; it does not itself reduce the total stock.Three quantities must be kept distinct. is the identification of a vulnerability. is its public reporting. is its effective removal from the software.CVE counts track a subset of publicly recorded vulnerabilities. They miss vulnerabilities found and fixed internally without public assignment of an identifier.Residual vulnerability stock is also not the same as residual security risk. Severity, exploitability, exposure, and available mitigations matter. A hundred obscure issues in unreachable code may represent less practical risk than one remotely exploitable flaw in an exposed service.One curve describes the rate at which vulnerabilities are discovered. Another describes the residual stock of vulnerabilities that remain.These curves do not necessarily move together.A surge in discoveries can coexist with a falling residual stock if vulnerabilities are eliminated faster than new ones are introduced. Conversely, a low discovery rate can coexist with a stable or growing vulnerability stock if scrutiny is limited or remediation lags. The discovery curve alone cannot establish whether software is becoming more secure.Public CVE disclosures provide an imperfect observable indicator of the first curve, not a direct measurement of it.In open source, the discovery curve is hypothesized to rise earlier and more sharply for three reasons:First, source code makes large-scale AI-assisted analysis easier, although AI can also analyze binaries.Second, open-source code is generally accessible to independent researchers and automated systems, while proprietary binaries, historical versions, and patches may be less readily available.Third, open-source discoveries and remediation are often more publicly visible, while proprietary vendors can handle some findings internally before public disclosure.This could also produce a more visible peak in public disclosures, although the two trajectories need not be identical.A further accelerator is independent scrutiny by downstream users. Open-source projects are not analyzed only by their maintainers or security researchers. Commercial manufacturers and integrators also have incentives to examine the components they depend on, reinforced by regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act, which establishes security responsibilities across their software supply chains. AI makes such analysis increasingly affordable and repeatable. Even a small project could therefore face continuous scrutiny from many independent organizations, accelerating the discovery of historical vulnerabilities while helping detect new ones before another backlog accumulates. Projects that can keep pace may become substantially more secure. Those that cannot may struggle to survive.The same visibility can accelerate independent investigation and remediation through upstream fixes, forks, and downstream patches without waiting for a single vendor.Neither advantage is guaranteed.Limited maintainer capacity can turn a discovery surge into a growing backlog of known but unfixed vulnerabilities. Well-resourced proprietary vendors may remediate internal findings faster.Proprietary software could experience a lower, later, and less visible peak in public vulnerability statistics. But that does not necessarily imply a lower rate of actual discovery. Its source is generally available to fewer external researchers, while well-resourced vendors can conduct extensive internal AI-assisted analysis, discover vulnerabilities, and remediate them before public disclosure.Furthermore, delaying discovery does not eliminate the underlying vulnerabilities. If the historical backlog is examined and remediated more slowly, vulnerabilities may remain undiscovered and unfixed for longer. A lower public disclosure rate, reflected in fewer CVEs, can therefore coexist with a larger hidden vulnerability backlog, although extensive internal security analysis by proprietary vendors can change that outcome.A hidden vulnerability backlog is not necessarily a safer one. Public disclosure can increase immediate exploitation risk by enabling parallel attacks, but it also creates an opportunity for remediation. Once a vulnerability is effectively eliminated, that particular exposure ends. By contrast, vulnerabilities that remain undiscovered or unremediated can persist for years, while attackers may independently discover and exploit them without any public disclosure. If broader AI-assisted scrutiny allows open-source projects to discover and eliminate their historical vulnerabilities earlier, they may accept greater short-term exposure in exchange for fewer long-term attack opportunities.AI can still analyze binaries, compare patched and unpatched versions, and probe running systems. Closed source is not immune. The practical difference is often whether an attacker has access to the binary itself or only remote interaction with a running system.Once sufficient technical information is available, unpatched deployments face similar exposure to AI-assisted exploitation regardless of the original licensing model. Proprietary vendors can still retain advantages in controlling the distribution of fixes and aspects of disclosure coordination.Closed source also rarely means pure closed source. Most commercial products depend on substantial amounts of open-source code, and many proprietary vendors participate in upstream projects.Those vendors cannot fully control the vulnerability discovery and disclosure timelines of their dependencies.AI-driven vulnerability discovery creates four immediate pressures—and a critical challenge:Misleading public metrics: A surge in reported vulnerabilities can make software appear less secure even while its residual vulnerability stock is declining.Compressed response windows: Exploitation can outpace patch development and deployment.Production deployment bottlenecks: Traditional testing, change management, and downtime requirements delay security updates.Regulatory and disclosure pressure: Vulnerability-handling obligations and coordinated disclosure add operational complexity.The critical challenge is having no time to adapt. Open-source communities, individual maintainers, and enterprise teams must adapt to security-response timelines far shorter than those they are accustomed to, while already facing an accelerating vulnerability flood. Many lack the automation, resources, or capacity to make that transition quickly enough.AI can shorten the time from discovery to exploitation. It can also shorten the time required to develop a fix.The production deployment lag, however, largely predates AI.Enterprise testing, validation, and change-management processes still take time. The danger is that attackers may increasingly exploit vulnerabilities faster than organizations can deploy remediation.Even when fixes are available, delays in processing security advisories and identifying affected downstream dependencies can postpone remediation before production deployment even begins ().As AI compresses the interval between discovery and exploitation, potentially to near zero, traditional response timelines become increasingly untenable. Maintainers may need to investigate, develop, validate, and release fixes within hours rather than days or weeks. Enterprises face the same pressure to test and deploy those fixes into production with minimal delay. For the most critical, readily exploitable vulnerabilities, security response may need to approach real-time operations rather than periodic patch management.The response must be to aggressively compress the traditional patch workflow from development to production. Automated QA, regression testing, and deployment validation can shorten the time needed to release fixes safely. Once fixes are available, technologies that minimize service disruption can accelerate their deployment into production: cloud-native workloads designed for rolling restarts without service interruption, user-space live patching beyond the Linux kernel, and high-availability clustering for traditional applications. The objective is not merely to produce patches faster, but to deploy them into production before attackers can exploit the vulnerabilities they address.Coordinated disclosure remains useful, but it cannot guarantee secrecy. Leaks, independent discoveries, public patch analysis, and active exploitation can all shorten the preparation window.Open-source communities can respond through parallel investigation, but actual response speed depends on available expertise, coordination, and maintainer capacity.When this discovery surge coincides with growing regulatory requirements, weaker projects, communities, and smaller companies may face genuine viability risks.The introduces security and vulnerability-handling obligations for covered products with digital elements, including requirements relating to vulnerability management, security updates, and reporting of certain actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents.These obligations do not apply uniformly. Non-commercial open-source development is treated differently from commercial products, while qualifying open-source software stewards have a distinct framework.Commercial vendors incorporating open-source components may nevertheless face obligations that increase expectations placed on upstream projects.Meanwhile, the cost of triaging genuine vulnerabilities alongside noisy, low-quality, or AI-generated reports can overwhelm limited maintainer capacity.Even projects that successfully improve their security may struggle with the financial and operational costs of the transition.Can All Open-Source Projects Survive?Open-source projects and maintainers will face five growing pressures: An unprecedented volume of vulnerability findings. Triage, prioritization, coordinated disclosure, and remediation.Continuous AI reassessment: Repeatedly scanning existing and new code as detection capabilities evolve. Helping downstream users deploy security fixes rapidly, including through compatibility with rolling updates, live patching, or high-availability environments where applicable. Continuously assessing the security and sustainability of critical third-party dependencies, particularly those maintained by small, underfunded communities.Together, these pressures increase the cost and complexity of maintaining open-source software, potentially beyond what smaller communities can sustain.The discovery flood will not affect every project equally. A well-funded project with dedicated security engineers, automated testing, and established vulnerability-response processes is in a very different position from a small community maintaining millions of lines of legacy code.Many widely used open-source dependencies are maintained by small, underfunded communities, sometimes by a single volunteer. This is not a new problem: critical software infrastructure often depends on projects with very limited maintenance resources, creating systemic dependencies whose importance far exceeds the capacity of the communities supporting them. The imbalance between commercial dependence on these components and financial support for their maintenance has been discussed for years.AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, combined with downstream compliance pressures from regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), could amplify this existing weakness. External researchers may soon be able to identify dozens of plausible vulnerabilities in days, while each report still requires validation, prioritization, remediation, and testing. Discovery capacity can scale dramatically without a corresponding increase in maintainer resources.Automation can help. AI-assisted initial triage, duplicate detection, reproducibility checks, and severity assessment can reduce the burden of processing vulnerability reports. Maintainers can prioritize issues according to exploitability, exposure, and practical impact rather than treating every reported finding as equally urgent.Integrating AI-assisted vulnerability detection into CI/CD pipelines can also prevent newly introduced vulnerabilities from accumulating into another historical backlog. But this addresses the future flow of vulnerabilities, not the immediate cost of investigating and remediating decades of existing defects.Continuous security reassessment also introduces a recurring cost. As AI detection capabilities evolve, projects will need to re-examine existing code, not just newly introduced changes. Running increasingly sophisticated analysis, validating findings, and maintaining the necessary infrastructure will require resources that smaller communities may struggle to sustain.The pressure extends beyond discovering and fixing vulnerabilities. Projects may also need to make security updates easier for their users to deploy, reducing the operational friction that leaves known vulnerabilities unpatched in production. Depending on the software, this may require supporting rolling updates, user-space live patching, or integration with high-availability clustering. These capabilities can reduce service disruption, but developing, testing, and maintaining them adds another cost that not every project can absorb.And automation has limits. A project may receive more genuine findings than its maintainers can investigate, validate, fix, and release—even after substantially improving its processes.Some projects will adapt. Others may need additional commercial support, foundation funding, shared security infrastructure, or new maintainers. Some may not survive the transition.The ability to discover vulnerabilities is scaling faster than the capacity of every open-source community to remediate them.Improving the security of open-source software does not guarantee the survival of the projects maintaining it.The risk is systemic, not merely local to individual projects. A vulnerability in a widely reused, poorly maintained component can affect thousands of downstream products. The 2024 XZ Utils backdoor demonstrated how weaknesses in the maintenance and trust structure of a small upstream project could threaten major downstream projects, including Linux distributions, even though the incident involved a supply-chain compromise rather than an AI-driven vulnerability-discovery flood.Even if the upstream project disappears, its software may remain embedded in production systems without security maintenance. AI-assisted discovery could expose these shared weaknesses at scale, turning the limited remediation capacity of a small upstream community into a security bottleneck for entire software supply chains. Greater reliance on fewer surviving projects could further concentrate systemic risk.AI-driven vulnerability discovery may act as an evolutionary pressure on open source. Projects capable of adapting can emerge stronger and more secure, while those unable to keep pace risk disappearing. The result may be more secure surviving projects, but also a less diverse ecosystem with greater concentration of systemic risk.The discovery flood could leave four lasting consequences: Effective remediation reduces historical vulnerabilities, while continuous AI reassessment limits the accumulation of new ones.Higher security standards: Continuous AI analysis and faster, less disruptive remediation become normal expectations for software maintenance.A lower vulnerability discovery rate: Once the historical backlog is substantially examined, vulnerability discovery will stabilize at a lower, continuous rate.A less diverse ecosystem: Rising maintenance costs may favor well-funded projects while threatening smaller communities.The predicted discovery peak creates an opportunity for surviving projects to eliminate a substantial portion of their detectable legacy vulnerabilities. Whether that opportunity translates into improved security depends on sufficient remediation capacity.The security benefit extends beyond publicly disclosed vulnerabilities. Undiscovered or privately discovered vulnerabilities may already be exploitable, including by attackers who never disclose them. Eliminating the historical backlog therefore reduces potential attack opportunities, not merely future CVE counts. The value of earlier discovery and remediation is that vulnerabilities can be removed before attackers exploit them—or before additional attackers independently discover them.And if AI-assisted security analysis becomes a normal part of development pipelines, those projects may be less likely to accumulate comparable backlogs again.This transition will also raise the baseline expectations for software maintenance. Continuous AI-assisted security reassessment, automated vulnerability triage, and faster remediation will increasingly become standard practices rather than optional investments. Users will also expect security updates that can be deployed with minimal service disruption. Meeting these expectations will require sustained engineering investment, even after the initial vulnerability flood subsides.The most heavily scrutinized codebases may no longer be those with the largest remaining vulnerability stock. They may be those in which the greatest proportion of detectable historical defects has already been eliminated.Raw CVE counts would then become an increasingly misleading comparative metric.Comparing ecosystems by the number of vulnerabilities they report in a given year risks rewarding opacity and penalizing transparency.But the benefits may not be distributed equally.The projects that survive may increasingly be those backed by commercial vendors, large foundations, or organizations capable of sustaining continuous security operations.Open-source software could emerge more secure from the transition, while the ecosystem maintaining it becomes less diverse.These predictions are testable and falsifiable, but they concern different outcomes.The temporary discovery peak would be challenged if vulnerability discovery rates remain persistently elevated in mature, extensively analyzed codebases, or if continuous AI-assisted analysis fails to prevent newly introduced vulnerabilities from accumulating into another substantial backlog.The open-versus-closed-source trajectory would be challenged if proprietary ecosystems demonstrate equally early and extensive vulnerability discovery through internal AI-assisted analysis, rather than experiencing a delayed discovery wave.The long-term security improvement depends on effective remediation. It would be undermined if discovered vulnerabilities remain unfixed or if elimination fails to outpace the introduction of new vulnerabilities.A decline in reported CVEs alone would not prove depletion. It could reflect reduced research activity, changes in disclosure practices, or declining analysis coverage.A dramatic increase in reported vulnerabilities does not necessarily mean software is becoming less secure. It may mean that decades of accumulated defects are finally being found.Unlike the past, however, future software development could increasingly detect those defects before they become another generation of accumulated security debt.Whether this discovery wave leaves open source weaker or stronger depends on which projects and companies can convert the findings into fixes before the peak exhausts them.**The software reporting the most vulnerabilities today may be the software whose hidden vulnerabilities are disappearing fastest—provided it survives long enough for the cleanup to matter.**

item.title: Tesla to Wind Down Cybertruck Production
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Elon Musk says Tesla will be "winding down" Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory around mid-2027 to free up capacity for increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi. CNBC reports: The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company's plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward. Musk did not say whether the company would produce the Cybertruck at a different facility, but he later responded to a user on X who called the update an "end of an era" and said the Cybertruck was the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made." "True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time," Musk said.
The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk's pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000. "Trucks have been the same for a very long time," Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019. "Like 100 years. Trucks have been basically the same. We want to try something different." While Tesla does not break out its sales by model or region, Cox Automotive estimated sales of the Cybertruck last year at 20,237 units in the U.S., down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Thank you Slashdot reader Dan Posluns for sharing the news.

item.title: Britain to Make Salary Disclosure In Job Ads Mandatory
item.author: BeauHD
item.content:encoded:
Britain plans to require employers to disclose salaries in job advertisements. "Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement. Reuters reports: The government said requiring companies to disclose pay in job ads would help young people applying for their first jobs, while boosting pay transparency and helping tackle disparities that can disadvantage women. Just over two in five employers always publish salary ranges, while fewer than one in five always disclose specific salaries, Burnham's office said, citing estimates from the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development.
The government will soon introduce legislation to parliament making salary disclosures mandatory, Burnham's office said, although it did not provide a timeline. Nearly one million, or 13%, of 16 to 24 year-olds in Britain are not in employment, education or training, one of the highest shares in Europe. A government review into youth inactivity is due to be published later in November.

item.content:encoded: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Sony has brought back the MDR-3-series headphones that debuted in 1979 alongside the Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player. [...] The new MDR-3R (originally called the "MDR-3L2") headphones look just like the originals and come with orange and blue ear cushions. New headphones are often wireless these days, but the MDR-3R continues the wired tradition of the MDR-3, with an essential twist: a USB-C connector. For better or worse, the new headphones also use "the same 23 mm driver units as the MDR-3 to reproduce sound quality close to the original," per Sony. Audiophiles will prefer something more advanced, perhaps with additional acoustic features. In addition to the USB-C connector, the MDR-3R also adds an in-line remote control and an integrated microphone. They are available for $60.

item.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.One connection, works every time, needs no retriesThere are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.
